speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with an urgent matter of pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that coastal fishermen of groundfish in the Atlantic have received a special subsidy of two cents a pound up to October 1, 1978, which meant an assistance of $1.5 million in 1977-78, considering also that those coastal fishermen, as is the case in the Gaspe peninsula, cannot take advantage of the 200-mile zone and that they cannot always make both ends meet solely with fishing and finally owing to the unemployment rate in that group of the population, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO END STRIKE-LABOUR DISPUTES IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. The Canadian Union of Postal Workers has now formally declared a national strike. Ministers at various times have indicated that legislation would be introduced in this House to deal with that strike. As the Prime Minister will know, it is the normal practice of the government, when introducing emergency legislation of this kind, to consult the House leaders of the other parties and provide those House leaders with an advance copy of any legislation that is intended. That has not been done so far in this case.
Can the Prime Minister indicate to the House of Commons, now, whether it is the intention of the government to introduce legislation that will restore postal service in this country, and can he indicate whether the normal courtesies will be followed and an advance copy will be made available to the representatives of the other parties in this House?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO END STRIKE-LABOUR DISPUTES IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the normal moment during orders of the day we will give first reading to a bill dealing with the postal strike. The House leader will be consulting with the leaders of the other parties to see if we can obtain the consent of the House to proceed with that bill later today after members have had an opportunity to study the bill at first reading.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO END STRIKE-LABOUR DISPUTES IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister knows, from the undertaking given by my colleague, the opposition House leader, last Friday that this party is certainly prepared to give unanimous consent today to second reading of that legislation. 1 would hope that it would be possible for us to see that legislation, as is the normal practice, well enough in advance so there can be serious consideration of its implications prior to any debate.
My question relates to the more general problem of strikes in the public service and in essential services. The Prime Minister will know that since 1971 there have been 93 strikes by unions under the Public Service Staff Relations Act. He will know that on eight separate occasions since 1972 this parliament has been brought back to resolve disputes in the public sector.
In 1968, the Woods commission proposed the establishment of a Public Interest Disputes Commission. Against all this history, in the legislative agenda that the Prime Minister has said he has prepared for this parliament-of which we have seen very little evidence so far-is it the intention of the government to introduce legislation that will establish in practice a Public Interest Disputes Commission or some other forum that will reduce the extent to which parliament has to
October 17, 1978

intervene in labour management disputes affecting essential aspects of the public interest?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO END STRIKE-LABOUR DISPUTES IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition, as usual, put a lot of remarks in his question which have to be dealt with. First, he said his party would give unanimous consent to second reading even before seeing the legislation.

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO END STRIKE-LABOUR DISPUTES IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext: Tie did not say that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO END STRIKE-LABOUR DISPUTES IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Then he said he wanted to see the legislation; he reminded us that the House leader indicated the other day unanimous consent to legislation. All I said in my answer was that we would give first reading in a moment and that later today we would go to second reading. I do not see why the Leader of the Opposition has to make the point that he wants to look at the bill: that is exactly what I said we would do.
With regard to the strike record in the public service, there have been hundreds of settlements, without a strike-I believe the percentage is well below 10 per cent and is in the area of 5 per cent-of collective agreements which have had to go the strike route. Therefore, I think that situation does not reveal any note of panic.
The government has been called upon to act in certain circumstances. We have called parliament and even recalled parliament to deal with particular strikes which were deleterious to public order and the common good. We have dealt with them, and we intend to continue doing so in the future.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO END STRIKE-LABOUR DISPUTES IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to the Prime Minister, with all charity, that this is not exactly a day on which he should carry on in his general, traditional, disputatious way.

speechtext:

Last year, the minister announced on March 28 that he was setting up a royal commission of inquiry into transportation in Newfoundland, and he said then that there would be no lay-offs by the CN and no changes until the royal commission made its final report.
Has the minister received telegrams from the Newfoundland government and from the railway transportation unions advising him that CN has now cancelled certain trains between St. John's and Corner Brook and is going to lay off 20 men as a result, and will the minister order CN to follow his directions, to put that train back as scheduled, to stop the lay-off of these 20 men and to observe his directions as they were given in March of 1977?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: RAIL SERVICE IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Sullivan commission recommendation itself indicated that for at least the next five years every effort should be made to cause the railway to run effectively and efficiently-or more so than in the past-in Newfoundland and that the final decision about the future of the railway should be taken at that time. Obviously, the implication of the Sullivan commission recommendation is a matter which will be discussed with the provincial government in relation both to the railway and to the highway as well as many other matters, so that these matters will be given very close attention in the very near future. We, of course, will want a final report from the Sullivan commission in connection with those discussions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at ten o'clock last night I was discussing the decline of the timber trade in the Ottawa valley at the turn of the
The Address-Mr. Hopkins
century. I went on to discuss how, at that stage, the federal government started moving in to fill the economic gap and how, in 1907, Camp Petawawa was established.
Forest research started on a 38-square mile area of Camp Petawawa in 1917. This contradicts many reports I have read in the media where the area has been reported as 36 acres or 38 acres; it is exactly 640 times that, being 38 square miles.
In the mid 1940s the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, under the St. Laurent administration started what is today the Atomic Energy of Canada Limited nuclear research laboratories at Chalk River, with Deep River as a major residential community for that Crown corporation. In 1970 the area was designated as a special area for growth incentives by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Much of this development program was based on the forest products industry. A general development subagreement was signed for the upper Ottawa Valley by the federal and provincial governments on December 7 last year to provide for infrastructure and special projects for economic development. This has been of major importance to the economic base of the Ottawa Valley.
Additional employment programs were introduced and applied by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), many of which are related to the major developments already mentioned, and have meant a great deal to us.
At the beginning of my speech I mentioned the original three staples on which Canada was founded, fur, timber, and wheat. As a result of the recent public demands for cut-backs, with which 1 agree, as governments cannot go on spending at the expense of the private sector forever, the Petawawa Forest Experimental Station has been proposed as one of the cuts. I disagreed with this specific cut very strongly from the start, and still do so. Forestry research in Canada is essential if we are to plan responsibly for future generations of Canadians.
It is well known that the Minister of State for the Environment (Mr. Marchand) is a very strong supporter of forestry, and it is unfortunate that his department should suffer so much from the cutbacks in research. It is in the public interest that he be assisted by myself and other members of parliament, by the provincial governments-and the public, in this difficult financial position, and I intend to do everything possible to that end. This must be done in a rational and responsible manner. Part of that rationale must be that the forests of Canada be looked upon as a continuing strong staple product of our country. We cannot afford to lose our expertise and technological know-how in the forest research field, any more than we could afford the cancellation of the Arrow aircraft by the last Conservative government with the resulting loss of experts and technologists to the aviation industry. If the Arrow had been allowed to go ahead this government would not now be in the position of having to spend the $2.34 billion in 1977 that is proposed for the purchase of new fighter aircraft because the Arrow would still be considered a modern aircraft.
The argument can be made very effectively and realistically that the investment, which a federal or provincial government

October 17, 1978
The Address-Mr. Hopkins
puts into forestry research and management is returned several times over in revenue dollars, employment, and international trade. If our forest research and development and management research programs are allowed to go ahead unscathed, it will spell a greater future for the forestry industry in Canada and will mean more revenue for the government.
Just what does forestry mean to Canada and its provinces? In this respect many of the letters I have received show that provincial governments that have a large interest in forestry have not gone unscathed either. Before I deal with what the forestry industry really means to Canada I would like to inform the House and the people of Canada that the mail I have received as a spokesman on this issue-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How did you get it?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I can tell the hon. member that I am delighted to have received it. It outnumbers the total amount of the mail I received on the issue of the death penalty by five to one. This is a healthy sign, as it shows the people of this country are still concerned about their forestry, that they want research and development, good forest management, and that they are right on key on this subject.
At a glance, what does the forest industry mean to the economy of Canada? Three hundred thousand people are directly employed in the forest industry in this country, and the total number of people employed directly and indirectly is one million, or 11 per cent of the total labour force in Canada. The value of products from all forestry industries is $4,600 million. The forest industry accounts for 20 per cent of our total exports or international trade. In other words, 20 per cent of all of the exports from this country are from forest based industries.
We produce 40 per cent of the world's newsprint. As far as the balance of trade is concerned, the forest products of Canada provide $4 billion toward our balance of trade in international sales. Revenue Canada receives approximately $1 billion in revenue from the forest industry in Canada. The provincial governments receive approximately $650 million in revenue, and it cannot be forgotten that they control the Crown lands and the timber sales. The federal share of total forest revenue, and this is made up by taxation on corporations and income taxes from employees etc. represents two-thirds of the total revenue from this industry the remainder is taken in by the provinces. The percentage of total revenue for Canada is 4 per cent in that one industry alone.
The budget of the Canadian Forestry Service is approximately $35 million. Herein lies the basis for my argument that with the federal treasury receiving $1 billion in taxation from forest based industries, and the provincial governments receiving $650 million from the forest industry, we have only about $35 million going into the Canadian Forestry Service which makes up the total research programs.
The Petawawa Forest Experimental Station is the oldest forest experiment station in Canada. It has a world-wide

reputation in forestry. This is why it is no local matter. It is even becoming a matter of national and international discussion. Indeed it would be a tragic loss to forest science. It is the best documented forest in Canada, and this is quite in keeping with the traditional timber trade and the economically based forestry industry of the valley. If the station is closed there is no way that the upwards of 61 years invested in time and research could be recouped.
In my earlier days as a teacher-I started teaching in an area where the forest was the very basis of the local economy. That took place in some of those beautiful hill-covered townships of Lyndock, Brudenell, Sabastopol, Radcliffe, Raglan, Griffith, etc. in the county of Renfrew. If we are going to renew those forests on the hillsides, and if we renew the forest on low grade land in the traditional forest areas of Canada, we must have timber based on the more rapid growth system. Some of this work and advice has come from the Petawawa Forest Experimental Station. They deal very closely with provincial governments and their natural resource departments. In particular, they have been in close liaison with the Department of Natural Resources of Ontario. The recent general development subagreement announced for the lower part of the Ottawa Valley in Eastern Ontario with regard to rapid growth wood for the pulp and paper industry was developed partly on scientific and technological advice from the Petawawa station in co-operation with the Department of Natural Resources in Ontario.
We get all kinds of mail today about every phase of Canadian life and every issue that arises. So, because I have a very sentimental and in depth feeling for the forest resources of our country and for the people who make their living there, I must say that I appreciate to the nth degree all those many letters I have received from elementary school children who print or write their letters, through to high school students, and university students who have studied at the experimental station and who are interested in the Canadian Forestry Service.
I have received three letters from abroad, also many from people who have visited the station and people who have done experimental work at the station. I have received letters from the professional foresters' groups, as well as from the general public across Canada. This mail has been largely generated by the public awareness program operating at the station. The station can be seen as you drive up the valley. Tours are available. Last year 15,000 students came through the forestry station. I have also had letters from people across Canada who happened to be travelling through and visited the station this year or other years. They read in the press about the cutback and that the station was to be closed. These people are totally in disagreement with this decision.
The Petawawa Forest Experimental Station is concerned with research into management of natural and manmade forests. Forest fire is a very important part of their research work. This is important. What is the use on the one hand of developing very rapid growth of trees, or developing a better quality of tree, if we do not at the same time upgrade our ability to fight forest fires?
October 17, 1978

There is a strong program in tree genetics. They are known internationally for their tree seed. The Petawawa Forest Experimental Station is concerned with research into interpretation techniques and audience response, and also the use of forests for energy production and conservation, which is another important phase of our modern-day life. They go into interpretation, demonstration, technology transfer, and consultation.
Provision is made for facilities for research, recreation, conferences and education for the following: federal government centres, that is the Insect Pathology Research Institute, the Forest Fire Research Institute, and the E. Forest Products Laboratory; universities and schools; and the local community. This includes swimming, fishing, hunting, skiing, etc. because it is located in one of those lake and woods areas of the valley. Provincial governments deal with them constantly, as I mentioned, as well as the commercial forest industry.
If there is one thing I want to make clear it is this: I do not feel that there has been enough co-ordinated effort in Canada with regard to the forest industry on the part of those interested in the forests of Canada to form a proper lobby. This lobby is not only needed for a big crash campaign or at a time when a crisis arises in the Canadian forest experiment stations, but it is needed on a continuing basis to support and promote the Federal Forestry Service and provincial programs.
I understand the province of Ontario has drastically cut back on its budget for the department of natural resources. We cannot go on this way forever and still expect our forests to remain viable for future generations.
My point is simply this. After this debate is over, we cannot stop there. There must be a strong lobby by professional foresters. Strong corporations must also be involved. Surely their interests are tied up in this as well. Possibly they are going to neglect the forest industry and put their money in some other business.
In addition, there are the small sawmills and veneer plants in designated and depressed areas. In northern Ontario, 82 per cent of the people gain their livelihood from the forest industry. The components of the forest management policy are many and varied in nature. The Reed report entitled "Forest Management in Canada" made the following recommendations:
1.	Tree Improvement: The introduction of genetically superior stock is intended.
2.	Protection: Fire protection is reasonably well cared for now.
I would add, Mr. Speaker, that it must be continued.
Protection from insects is inadequate to cope with large scale epidemics such as the spruce budworm.
In this day when we are talking about conservation, it bothers me to see elm trees along our rural roads, victims of Dutch elm disease, being left to rot. They should be harvested. This is another reason-masses of dead trees-why forest research programs must be continued. With $35 million going into the Canadian forestry service and $1,650 million going
The Address-Mr. Hopkins
into the federal and provincial treasuries, surely we could do better. It would not take that much more and the return on investment would be many times the original expenditure.
I again quote from the Reed report:
3.	Research and Development: Primary research should be stepped up and in some cases redirected. There is an additional need for applied research and large-scale operating trials of various silvicultural treatments.
4.	Canadian Forestry Service: This agency requires a status in accordance with the contribution of forestry to the national economy and its budgets should be restored in order to play its legitimate role in an expanded program of forest management.
That is precisely the point I was making a moment ago.
An expanded program of primary research is called for across the board. Stand improvement and tree improvement hold great promise, but related research has not kept pace with regeneration studies. The federal government should re-establish the priorities in this area which were sacrificed in favour of environmental studies.
Reed further calls attention to serious regional problems in five provinces aggravated by the ravages of spruce budworm, by forest area withdrawals resulting from environmental pressures, and by shortfalls in forest management.
In making these recommendations, Reed alludes to many constraints in achieving improvements in forest management intensity. He alludes to the complexity of planning framework, the lack of general expanded commitment in forest management, and the existence of intense rivalry between federal and provincial governments. That is unfortunate. It should not be. There should be a total spirit of co-operation, with the provinces playing their role in co-operation with the federal government.
There is open friction interdepartmentally in Ottawa and in the separate provincial capitals, and even within individual resource ministries at the provincial level. There is a need for a mechanism to co-ordinate forestry programs of private industry and senior governments with identification of management priorities through to implementation and funding.
There is a need for appreciation of the forest sector as one of Canada's most important generators of activity. That is something I alluded to as a long-term program. It has been with this country since day one. Only a rational approach to research and development in forest management, pest control and disease control will continue this growth.
Net imports of the United States, mostly from Canada, are expected to increase from a roundwood equivalent of 1.6 billion cubic feet in 1972 to 2.8 billion cubic feet by the year 2000. Canada is presently the world's largest exporter of forest products, with approximately 10 per cent of the world's productive forest land area, and growing stock reserves. The forest land must be replanted with upgraded timber.
If we can succeed in improving the quality of our timber resource in Canada, the manufacturer will have lower production costs at his mill or plant. This in turn will make him more competitive on the international market. It will help retain that 20 per cent of the international market. Indeed, for the first quarter of 1978, forest products in Canada represented something like 32 per cent of our international trade.

No more applicable words could be applied to the circumstances of today than those which were used in the Holy Scripture of thousands of years ago.

One thing that the Prime Minister wishes for today is that there would be an amendment to the law which would extend the period of five years between elections. He said he had been in Morocco for 20 days. I said that it seemed even longer than that. I said that I was going to deal with the economy, but I am not, because it has been fully dealt with already. However, I do not think that Canadian people fully realize what a spendthrift government there is in existence. The Prime Minister speaks of restraint. Last year the deficit was $13 billion. This year it is expected to go as high as $15 or $16 billion. It will take years for this country to re-establish itself in so far as national finance is concerned. The government has earned the description of "Trudeau squandermania". That is what it has done, and that is why the Prime Minister leaves the House so quickly, because he knows he cannot face a debate. It is easy for him to make general statements, but 1 would have liked the opportunity to ask him some questions so that he could answer them immediately.
I come now to a question that is of great concern to me, and that is the monarchy. He has endeavoured all through the years to destroy the monarchy and to bring about a republic in Canada. The other day in the House he stated, as reported at page 37 of Hansard:
We are repeating, Mr. Speaker, and we have said it since 1968, that this is the intention. The intention was explained to Her Majesty at Buckingham Palace by the then minister of justice and she saw it that way too.
That statement is false, because the Queen must accept whatever recommendation her prime minister has made. To pretend that she was in favour of this indicates on his part a desire to contravene the basic principles of parliamentary government. Now he says that he does not intend to have the right hon. member for Prince Albert along with the Leader of the Opposition misinterpret his views as to what he intends to do. If that were true I would be the first to admit it.
Let us look at the views of Senator Eugene Forsey, a Liberal and one of the great constitutional experts of Canada. He said, as reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail of July 24, 1978:
-he will fight Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau's proposed constitutional changes to the limit.
Mr. Forsey... called the constitutional package such a "weird concoction" ... Mr. Trudeau's proposals would turn Canada into a republic and make the Queen a sort of deputy to the Governor General-
That is the view I have been expressing and that is the view of the constitutional experts.
The Prime Minister set out to get rid of the Senate because he knows he cannot abolish the monarchy and have both the House of Commons and the Senate. So, he starts this institution which will be neither fish nor fowl but will end the Senate. Where do the senators stand? I quote from an amendment to the motion by the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution:
That this committee report to the Senate and the House of Commons its concern with the position of the government to the effect that it can proceed unilaterally, that is, by a mere law of parliament, with the provisions of Bill C-60 respecting the Senate of Canada and the position of the Crown, and-
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
Let us see how many of the Liberal senators voted yea: Forsey, Fournier, Bird, Denis, Lang, Langlois, Mcllraith and Neiman.
Mr. Mcllraith came into the House of Commons at the same time that I did. He is a man for whom I have had intense admiration all through the years. He never deceived or used double language, and I do not mind being associated with people like that at all. All these Liberals said that the plan was wrong.
The Prime Minister has said that he is going to make the Senate an extinct species. Now, however, he says that he loves the monarchy, that, "Why, the very suggestion that he is trying to tear it down shocks his finer sensibilities". I will read what he had to say, because he has not changed from 1940 to 1978. All through the years it has been condemnation of the monarchy. He said on March 5, 1976, while speaking to the provincial congress of the Liberal Party of Canada in Quebec city in effect that as long as he is around all will be well.
He goes on to say that there are three sides to the constitutional question. There is a division of powers that we have not been able to solve, there is the amending formula, but most important of all there is what people call the repatriation. Basically, this means we are going to take away from England, the United Kingdom, this foreign country, although it is a friend-he actually goes that far-the right to make laws for Canadians. They have never made any laws for Canadians; the British North America Act simply provides that the amendments asked for by the Parliament of Canada will be accepted. In the next sentence he says:
Do you think that the Queen of England will tell Bourassa: admit that Trudeau is right or tell me, admit that Bourassa is right? ... We must agree to tell the English to stop making laws for us.
That is a dastardly statement and very false.
I am going to get the constitution back and when I get it back we'll be able to form in this country a new kind of government and I shall be the first to appoint the first President of Canada in the person of Jules Leger, or of Hughes Lapointe.
That is what he said. That is his purpose. The other day he falsified his position, because he can turn somersaults faster than anyone who has ever occupied the position of prime minister.
What does he do? He gets caught and, whenever he gets caught, he follows Machiavelli who is referred to as his patron. Machiavelli says if you have to change your views, people forget. He says today he will get the constitution back, but let me read what he said on May 20, 1964. He and the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde), he and a group of French Canadian intellectuals, produced a manifesto, translated by Michael Pitfield who is today, among other things, the secretary of the Privy Council.
The derangement resulting from nationalism is particularly revealed today by the exaggerated importance given by our leading citizens to constitutional problems.
Constitutional problems in Canada are far from being so serious or so important as some would have us believe. The obstacles to economic progress, to
October 17, 1978

full employment, to an equitable welfare scheme or even to the development of French culture in Canada, are not principally the result of the Canadian Constitution.
The restraints are not judicial but social and economic in nature. It is an exaggerated conception of the power of the written word that believes that these restraints will be wiped away as a result of mere constitutional change, whatever its magnitude.
The so-called building of a new constitutional structure is as futile as a a huge game of blocks and the effort devoted at the present time to debating such a reform takes up a great deal of energy that could be profitably spent in solving much more fundamental problems in our society.
Take your choice; one statement today, another tomorrow.
I am going to make a prediction, Mr. Speaker, and I do not often do that. He is scared out of his wits over the Senate. He is frightened. Those senators-Forsey, almost immortal while yet a mortal-and others who stood with him-I have named some of them and there are more-they have him frightened. I have no doubt whatever that one of these days he will withdraw that portion of the so-called constitutional package connected with the Senate.
What else is he going to do? No longer is there going to be a cabinet. It is not going to be called a cabinet but a council of state. That is the French expression.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for this opportunity to take part in the throne speech debate. Like the previous speakers, I would like first of all to congratulate the co-movers of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. members for York South (Mrs. Appol-loni) and for Verdun (Mr. Savard). I also wish to express my admiration for His Excellency the Governor General and Madame Leger who performed their duties with a selflessness and a simplicity that warmed the hearts of all Canadians. I also want to congratulate the new generation of House of Commons pages. 1 hope that every one of us will give them the attention they deserve.

October 17, 1978
The Address-Mr. Allard
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments about the rhetoric and the criticisms aimed by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at the Leader of the Opposition. While we were beginning to see the right hon. Prime Minister as a financial wizard going into battle, as he has said so often in English, with his three weapons, the three Rs, that is Restraint, Reallocation and Renewal, we now discover a philosopher who tells us about the three Fs, that is the three faculties of the brain: memory, imagination and intelligence. He generously granted the first two to the Leader of the Opposition but kept the third for himself. As the saying goes, "Charity begins at home".
Mr. Speaker, the opposition may well have a lot of imagination, but it would perhaps be wise and not such a bad thing if the government also had some. As for memory, since I have been in this House, we have not stopped telling the government what its duty should be in view of the present economic situation. To go on in the same spirit, I would like to speak about what I myself call the three Fs, that is the three failures of the government-unemployment, inflation and the endless federal-provincial conflicts with the federal government imposing its will on everyone without ever trying to obtain a consensus. What is there in this Speech from the Throne that deserves our confidence? After reading it several times, I still wonder where we are going. As concerns the most serious current problem, unemployment, even though we may try reading between the lines, we can foresee little hope of improvement. The government says that it will help the private sector, even though it is badly weakened, to give a new impetus to the economy. We are told that at the summit meeting held in Bonn, Canada committed itself to give work to all Canadians. We are told that the objective of the government employment strategy is to encourage job creation in the private sector. The employment strategy, Mr. Speaker, is something new. At last the government has an employment strategy. We do not know much about the way it works, but there is actually an employment strategy, and that is reassuring, Mr. Speaker. There are 946,000 unemployed in Canada, including 301,000 in Quebec. Given the fact that out of that number 263,000 are going to be withdrawn from unemployment rolls and increase the number of people on welfare, Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) still intends to go ahead with his project of cutting expenses, the government of Quebec might find itself, after these cuts, with a substantial additional burden in the area of social assistance. But which type of industries are going to be granted these additional funds that the government is going to invest in job creation? That is the big question. Heavy industry, oil industry and major industrial centres. What will happen to economically underprivileged areas like mine, and the whole Gaspe area? I would like to quote the Quebec minister of labour who said on September 7 last:

The funds intended for those programs could be directed toward the areas most likely to attact them, namely Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia.
The dilemma would be that the benefits of 90,000 unemployed Quebeckers would remain in Ottawa and end up in the richer provinces. We had a small example recently in the Ford Company which located in Ontario with a subsidy of $68 million. So, Mr. Speaker, we should ask the provinces, the
946,000	unemployed, the civil servants or the have-not regions what they think of the government's employment strategy. I think that yesterday about 10 per cent of the people answered flatly what they thought of the government's strategy and the present situation. Of course, the Prime Minister keeps repeating that everything is fine, thank you. Inflation is less severe here than in other countries. We are creating more jobs than any other country. We have a high standard of living. And he throws a bunch of figures our way, as he did in Winnipeg on September 18, and as he did once again in the House last week, telling us that 91 per cent of households in Canada have hot water, 90 per cent have showers, and 29 per cent have home freezers. And then he tells us that he has figures on flush toilets and sewers.
Mr. Speaker, I think that we have to be more serious than that. It is not a matter of knowing whether Canadians have outhouses or flush toilets but of knowing whether there will be jobs for our 946,000 unemployed. That unemployment is the very consequence of the economic slump we have been in for the past ten years. There will always be politicians like the Prime Minister to tell us that in spite of staggering unemployment, runaway inflation, a weak private sector, bankruptcies, endless labour conflicts, like at the Post Office, government quarrels like that sales tax business which made us lose two months in sterile debates, to tell us that in spite of all that, everything is fine.
I would like to take this opportunity to point out once again the growing gap between have and have-not regions. Last Friday the hon. member for Matane (Mr. de Bane), depicted a gloomy picture of the real situation in the Gaspe Peninsula. It is a sad reality, Mr. Speaker. What the hon. member from Matane tried to tell people in the area is that because they have been blindly loyal to an old party, particularly the Liberal party during the last 30 years, they should stop voting Liberal and change their political philosophy if they want to see better days. Indeed all the difficulties they are now facing, including unemployment and inflation, are the prize they get for their faithful loyalty to the old party, particularly to the Liberal party.
It is altogether inconceivable that budget cutbacks concerning government offices and unemployment benefits shold not be used to launch some make-work program. According to a Statistics Canada report, eastern Quebec had a 15 per cent unemployment rate. If we want to be more realistic, we should talk about an actual and permanent unemployment rate of 25
October 17, 1978

per cent. In some municipalities 50 per cent of the labour force is idle. That is because of lack of economic planning, investments, basic equipment, closing of plants, seasonal activities and so on. Those are some of the reasons for our difficulties.
For instance, in eastern Quebec we have mining, forest and marine resources that can we develop only if we have a share of foreign markets. The few industries and mines we have either reduced their production or ceased their operations because of that lack of opportunities. Many sawmills have closed down. As concerns fisheries, Gaspe does not benefit from the 200-mile limit as its industry is still based on inshore fishing. This is why this morning I put a question to the minister and proposed a motion asking him to maintain the 2 cents a pound subsidy to the Atlantic coast fishermen.
The tourism industry has a period of operation of no more than two months which tends to discourage potential investors. What hopes have we left if the government does not offer a tax incentive policy to industries that might be tempted to open plants in those areas? Not only is our unemployment rate the highest in the province of Quebec but it is also the highest in Canada according to the latest figures published by Statistics Canada. We are the champions of unemployment, a title we share without any pride with another Quebec region, Abitibi-Temiscamingue. This situation has many serious economic and human effects. Lives are ruined, opportunities are lost, there is bitterness, shame and we even had suicides. The economic consequences are very serious too: the loss of a countless number of man-years, a heavier welfare and unemployment insurance burden. It is the same on the social aspect: exodus of young people, the aging of the population and poverty.
Mr. Speaker, I have dealt almost exclusively with unemployment as I consider this problem crucial and urgent if we want to ensure the economic future of our country which is looking ever less promising. Unemployment reaching alarming proportions, inflation, the fall of our dollar, the highest interest rates in our history, those are many reasons for concern. And the right hon. Prime Minister tries to convince us that nevertheless everything is fine. I know that the Prime Minister has made several trips to the eastern Quebec region and admired all the natural beauties of Gaspe. I strongly suggest he should go back to our area and discover that other Gaspe peninsula he does not seem to know. Hopefully he will come back with other figures than those concerning flush toilets. We have good people, people with a lot of memory, a sincere memory, creative imagination and fruitful and honest intelligence, people still haunted by promises of a just society.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to commend the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) who moved concurrence in the throne speech. Thousands of Canadians heard that speech filled with sincere hope and dignity. That speech, made by the hon. member from York
The Address-Mr. M. Roy
South in the name of millions of citizens who also chose to emigrate to Canada, where they could have a full measure of human dignity and civil liberties, reminded us we need real strength rather than dead wood, Canada needs enthusiasm and belief rather than apathy to keep on developing its potential. I am so much prouder of that contribution that as a member I also repesent a constituency with a number of ethnic groups. They chose Canada for the same reasons. Some wanted to escape the tyranny of certain dictatures, others came because their home had been threatened or destroyed by wars, or to flee racism. Whatever the reason or reasons for leaving their country of origin and coming to a new country, there is unanimity that Canada offers them the opportunity of full development.
This is why on October 8, 1971, Prime Minister Trudeau tabled in the House a document on the main programs related to maintaining and developing multiculturalism across Canada. This document contained the decisions taken by the Liberal government following the recommendations in the report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. By creating a department to implement the recommendations made by the commission, the Liberal party proves that multiculturalism in a bilingual framework seems the best way to preserve the cultural freedom of Canadians. Thanks to this type of policy, discrimination and jealousy between different cultures should be eliminated. If national unity is to have a deep personal impact, it has to be based on each individual's feelings about his own identity. This might pave the way for mutual respect and views sharing among Canadians. A dynamic policy on multiculturalism will help us acquire this self confidence which could be the linchpin of a society which would guarantee equality and respect to all its people.
Consequently, I would like to point out that the Liberal government considers that multiculturalism in a bilingual society contributes to ensure the individual his freedom of choice.

I would like to point out a statement made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) relating to this important matter. 1 quote from a Canadian Press news report on the front page of the December 30, 1977, edition of the Toronto Star, under the headline "Joe Clark: Here's what I would do if I were PM" The following paragraph will be of concern to all Canadians on non-English, non-French origin:
Clark vowed to reorganize and trim the federal bureaucracy. He said he would take a hard look at abolishing the departments of fitness and amateur sport, multiculturalism and urban affairs.
That is the official statement by the Leader of the Opposition concerning the importance of multiculturalism.
[ Translation]
We are free to be ourselves but we cannot rely on chance, we must protect and seek that freedom. If it is jeopardized

October 17, 1978
The Address-Mr. M. Roy
among some ethnic groups, it can be jeopardized everywhere. In Canada and in the world, liberalism rests on the protection of the rights of the individual. Individuals will be able to attain maximum fulfillment only if they are allowed to fully exercise their rights in a climate of freedom and equality, the very idea of liberalism. Personal freedom, political freedom, equality and economic justice are all conditions favouring and garan-teeing those rights. They are at the core of the concern of the supporters of liberalism and the main subject of attention on the part of the Liberal Party of Canada.
The government, in creating the position of a minister responsible for multiculturalism, wish to encourage the development of our various ethnic groups, recognizing their contribution to the fabric of the Canadian nation. It is obvious that success in the development of such a program depends on the co-operation of the provinces as well. In my opinion, a legislation such as Bill 101 in Quebec does nothing to support the objectives pursued by the Canadian government. I seriously wonder about that and it seems that unfortunately this legislation tends to polarize French-speaking Canadians against English-speaking Canadians, not only in Quebec, Mr. Speaker, but across Canada. We just have to listen to comments, to read editorials and to study our financial pages to realize the importance of this situation.
Canada is now at the crossroads. It is regrettable to think that the future of this extraordinary country, a country where freedom is part of our heritage owing to various people who settled here, can be jeopardized by a possible separation of Quebec, a possibility which I hope will be rejected by the majority of Quebeckers who are looking for security, for the protection of their democratic freedoms, for social stability and for economic progress and by all those who intend to live from coast to coast in their own way, and as fully as possible, sharing Canadian wealth together.
The hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Savard) who has had the privilege to second the Address in Reply to Speech from the Throne has made us aware of the matters which concern his voters, of the particular interest he has for the elderly and of the importance of a continued improvement by joint efforts with the provinces, in the services to which they are entitled in the field of housing, transportation and medical care.
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and some of his colleagues and I have been disappointed by the rather gray image they cast throughout Canada. They project the image of a country plagued with unemployment by not mentioning the fact that 240,000 new jobs have been created in Canada every year over the past five years. Members of the opposition are much quieter and even mute when it comes to explaining the causes and suggesting remedies.
This situation must be clearly straightened out. Let us quote figures, absolute figures. One must consider that the labour force has grown by 308,000 in 1977 and 248,000 in 1976, which represents an increase of 3 per cent for 1977 and of 2.5 per cent for 1976.
Between 1965 and 1970, while the overall Canadian population increased by 1.6 per cent, the labour force expanded by 3.3 per cent. Between 1970 and 1975, the total population went up by 1.4 per cent while the labour force, people coming onto the labour market for the first time, grew by 3.5 per cent.
What are the projections for the period from 1981 to 1986? The total population is expected to go up by 1.3 per cent and the labour force by 1.7 per cent. In other words, a decline of more than 50 per cent in the labour force over the previous years. Statistics reveal that by 1985 we will probably experience a labour shortage.
Three quarters of this increase can be traced to the growing number of people old enough to work, the rest can be explained by the higher participation rate. Adult women in 1977 were the most important group in the 131,000 increase in the labour force; these women joined for most legitimate reasons, but they nevertheless increased its size. In other words, the labour force expands faster in Canada than in any other country in the world.
In a particularly difficult world situation we can proudly say that this country-every Canadian not only governments-has done as much, if not more, to create jobs and personal revenues, growth, development and investment as others in most countries of the world. But that has not been enough. Canada's performance has been remarkable compared with those of all OECD countries, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, which includes North America, Western Europe and Japan, and that was done in spite of the days lost through strikes in 1976, when we registered a loss of some 11,609,890 work days. We were one of the most affected countries in the world at that time and if we look at the situation in 1977, this figure was down to 3,829,750 days lost, which represents a rather significant improvement for 1978. Therefore we hope Canadians and unions will co-operate so we can continue to improve this situation.
On October 12, the right hon. Prime Minister quoted a series of statistics to establish a comparison with the United States and other OECD countries as regards job creation, social policies, real available net income per person living in Canada as compared with our American neighbour while the real disposable income per inhabitant increased from 100 to 151.9 per cent taking 1968 as the base year. In the United States that real net income increased from 100 to 124 per cent. Therefore, it means that we are ahead of our American friends. I do not intend to tell you that everything is for the best and that the government is not conscious of concerns in Canada.

October 17, 1978

The eight-point plan announced by the Prime Minister on August 1 last on his return from the Bonn summit conference and the contents of the Speech from the Throne make up an emergency plan for action combining several aspects of the government policy. It advocates speeding up action rather than taking a leap in the dark. It finally shows that the government is strongly determined to take imaginative measures recognizing that the priorities should be shifted, advocating restraint in government expenditures, the reallocation of funds in our social schemes and the renewal of funds used to urge private enterprise to create permanent jobs.
As for restraint, the government of Canada has always been blamed for the expansion of its budget. I have myself discussed during a review in committee the reasons warranting such and such an expenditure or questioned departmental officials about increased staff. I even asked for the establishment of productivity standards through an annual assessment of the staff, which is made today. You were right in making such a criticism. I was also right when I asked questions to the officials of various departments. We decided to reduce public expenditures by $500 million this year already and by $2 billion next year. For some people, it is not enough but it is an enormous amount for those who are affected. It was not easy if you consider the distribution of those funds.
For your information, let me point out that in the years 1961-1976 the distribution of the increases at the various levels of government as a percentage of the gross national product was as follows. In 1961, all the expenditures of the federal, provincial and municipal governments amounted to 30.8 per cent of the GNP whereas in 1976, they represented 40.3 per cent, an increase of 9 per cent. Now, let us have a look at federal expenditures including transfer payments to the provinces. That proportion was around 18 per cent in 1961 and became 20.2 per cent in 1976-an increase of only 2 per cent. Let us have a look now, if you want, at the increase in spendings at provincial and municipal government levels, excluding transfers. In 1961, these spendings represented 12.7 per cent of the gross national product whereas in 1976 they represented 20.1 per cent, that is an increase of 7.4 per cent. These figures may seem too high, but I think that public expenditures are also high. Here again, let us be careful before charging Ottawa for that situation, before thinking that all these finds are going to public servants who have nothing to do, or that it is just wasted money. Let us give back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, especially when Caesar has slowed down that alarming trend.
One sometimes hears certain people make comparisons with the situation in the United States, be it about taxation or other fields where Americans show a much more glossy picture than ours in the area of public expenses. Let us not forget that the main difference between Canadian and U.S. public service figures lies in the fact that health care in Canada rests with the public sector whereas in the United States it rests mostly
The Address-Mr. M. Roy
with the private sector, which accounts in the United States for a difference of 5 per cent to 6 per cent of their gross national product.
So I revert to this fact: for fiscal year 1975-76, federal payments to individuals amounted to $7.7 billion, of which almost 90 per cent paid as old age pensions, guaranteed income supplement, family allowances or unemployment insurance benefits-in fact, payments to individuals, to all Canadians, represent 22.8 per cent of the total federal budget.
We therefore had to cut back expenses without raising all sorts of objections, and we have redistributed funds among the lower income earners. This amendment allowed us to increase the garanteed income supplement by $20 a month per family, and some 3.3 million people will benefit from this measure. As the time allotted me is limited, I will not be able to complete the outline concerning family allowances, which have also been reviewed with a view to redistributing funds. I would recommend reading the leaflet that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) will send and in which she gives all the advantages and changes that have been brought to the family allowance program. Changes were also required in unemployment insurance. There are some people out of work who are really looking for a job, we are aware of that. However, upon further examination of the situation of unemployed people in Quebec, we have found that over 75 per cent of households affected by unemployment earn wages, that is to say, they have two sources of income, unemployment insurance benefits and wages which were not declared.
In fact, the latest data published by Statistics Canada on unemployment indicate that out of the 243,000 families, or
270.000	people, affected by unemployment in Quebec in the month of August, 184,000 had one or more sources of income and in 165,000 families, the breadwinner had work. This means that 59,000 families had no income at all, including
16.000	childless families. So we brought changes in the unemployment insurance scheme precisely to stimulate the development of Canada a little more.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with industry. I more particularly wish to thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) for the initiative he took when he was minister of industry, trade and commerce by talking the cabinet into signing the agreement with Canadair, an initiative that allowed hundreds of people of Laval and Montreal to work in the aeronautical industry and to participate in the development of the well known Challenger jet aircraft now being built by Canadair. That was a very important initiative for the metropolitan Montreal area, since 70 per cent of the total number of manufacturing jobs in the province of Quebec are concentrated in Montreal and since the economic health of the city has a considerable influence on the over-all economy of the province.
In the manufacturing industry, the jobless rate in Quebec has increased by 50,000, 41,000 of whom in the Montreal

October 17, 1978
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
area. This proposal is particularly worthy of attention because in the transport and aeronautics industries the Montreal area already has the basic facilities for further development of aircraft production. It will hopefully become a major centre for the transportation of all kinds of goods throughout North America.
Mr. Speaker, I will strongly support the proposal of the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Comtois), providing for further expansion in the northern area of Montreal in particular in Ste-Therese or the opening of a new Quebec General Motors plant in North Montreal. Considering that the bus plant will be built in Deux-Montagnes and that General Motors has already set up a car factory in Ste-Therese on the North shore, I will strongly support that move and call upon the municipal governments to back this very good proposal which will contribute to developing this sector of the motor industry in the northern part of Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, I also want to thank the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) who has agreed to designate the city of Laval, and include it in the special Montreal area which is eligible for industrial development grants of up to 25 per cent of the capitalization rate to set up new businesses and 20 per cent more to expand industries already existing, provided these businesses contribute $100,000. Already, Mr. Speaker, five new industries have received offers for a total amount of over one million dollars from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, for a total investment of approximately $10 million for the city of Laval.
I see my time is running out, and in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I remain optimistic for the future because the government has taken economic measures to meet the present needs, and with the determination of all Canadians, whether they work for private industry or the government or labour unions, we all have a part to play in meeting this challenge, in order to foster a real economic growth which will reflect the aspirations of all Canadians.

speechtext:
My good friend from Winnipeg says that maybe they did.
I am always very happy to follow the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), whom I have known for many years. He is a master in this chamber and one of the top orators who has entered this chamber in my time and, I am sure, in the experience of all others as well as in the experience

of those who were here before me. Having listened today to his witty good humour and noting his penetrating method in debate, there is no doubt that hon. members opposite listened very carefully. However, I must say that I was disappointed in the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde) and other backbench members of the Liberal party. When the right hon. gentleman asked for an extension of time, those hon. members said no to a former prime minister of this country. The right hon. member for Prince Albert is the only living former prime minister in this country, and the action of those hon. members was inexcusable.
Yesterday was quite a day. It was the day for by-elections. I suppose this might be a time for some elation and some celebration for our party, but above all it is a time to appreciate the democratic process of government. Many people in Canada, both inside and outside this House, believed that there would be an election last spring or this fall, but for one reason or another the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) lacked the courage necessary to call one. No doubt the people spoke with a loud, clear voice yesterday.
There is one thing about by-elections I like. They can be differentiated from Gallup polls. When voters speak in byelections, the result is accurate, assertive, and assessing. Therein lies the difference between the Gallup poll, which is often used in this nation, and a mini federal election of 15 by-elections. In the by-elections yesterday the people elected ten Progressive Conservatives, two New Democrats, two Liberals, and one Social Credit.
Thousands of words will be spoken and written about yesterday's by-elections, but for the Progressive Conservative party this is a time for sober thought. It is a time to appreciate that as a national party and the party of confederation we are on the verge of forming a new government for Canada. It is a time for us to accept the fact that governing this country will be very difficult. As described by our leader and also by the right hon. member for Prince Albert, at this time Canada is in an economic mess. The whole country seems unsettled, and disunity seems to be found everywhere.
I felt that the Ottawa Journal put it very accurately and adequately as follows:
On the basis of yesterday's returns, that challenge is simply beyond the reach of the Liberals under Mr. Trudeau. He could hardly have been more emphatically rejected than in the decisive loss of all five Liberal seats the party held in Ontario or in the sharp loss of popular vote strength shown across the board. The brave face Mr. Trudeau put on the matter of his personal acceptability as a leader was to be expected. But whether he takes the opportunity to reassess his own position, his party can hardly avoid facing the leadership question, and with urgency-
The result in Ottawa Centre, a smashing victory for the Conservatives, typifies their best hope in the months to come; to attract more high calibre candidates such as Robert de Cotret, and David Crombie who won so well in Rosedale, to leave the voters with no doubt that this is a party getting ready to govern. Finding such candidates will be a great deal easier starting today.
Therefore, I say at the outset, this is the time for this party to assess itself, it is the time to be most responsible and, above all, it is the time to continue-and I use the word advisedly-

to be credible, which we are. The proof that we are credible is the voters' confidence which was given to our national leader and to our party yesterday.
This is the time to appreciate our victory, but also the time to be humble-
