I am proud to say that much credit must be given to our national leader, a young man with great ability and lots of experience, a young man who has served at least two national leaders, the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert, our former national leader, and a premier, as well as serving his constituency here in the House of Commons. However, I was most disappointed when I heard here the other day the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), a former member of this party, a man whom I know very well, a man whose first nomination was held in Hanna in the constituency of Acadia, where I was guest speaker, now Crowfoot, who, I thought, sank to a new depth when he attacked personally the national leader of our party and referred in particular to his educational qualifications.
If you check very carefully you will see that our national leader has a Bachelor of Arts degree and a Master's degree in Arts. This seems to top the qualifications of the critic from Crowfoot. We do not know what grades he had in high school, but I do know he enjoyed a six weeks' extension course in the school of agriculture at one of the universities. At any rate, I suppose that when we come to discussing education, whether university or other, perhaps the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce can take some comfort from the fact that the late Sir Winston Churchill was not a university graduate, in spite of which he was probably one of the greatest leaders the world ever saw at a time of great crisis for the western world.
Now I would like to turn my attention and make some remarks with reference to the administration of justice. I was most disappointed to see that both in the Speech from the Throne and in the recent answers of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) it is evident that the question of law reform is now a forgotten chapter with this government. I should like to review with you, Mr. Speaker, for a few minutes the whole subject of crime and its causes.
When crime is on the increase, the notion that it can be described in a single category is erroneous. Violent crimes create a climate of fear in the streets of our growing cities. White collar crime, in economic terms, is much less visible than violent crime. The material cost of crime such as petty theft, consumer fraud, violations of the Combines Investigation Act, or embezzlement, dwarfs all crimes of violence.
Proper laws and proper law enforcement cannot be underestimated in the control of crime, but I have believed for years, not only as a member of parliament, but as a lawyer, that we
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
must launch an attack on the breeding grounds of crime. Crime breeds in the cesspools of injustice and poverty in the urban slums of our fast growing cities. The law must be just to be respected and obeyed. Urban poverty makes people who dwell in these cities the victims, not the masters, of their environment. Bad environment becomes the inheritance of the next generation. In order to launch a major assault on crime, we must attack conditions of despair and the denial of opportunity to people, which result in a growth in the incidence of crime. Today we have one million unemployed in Canada. That is a condition of despair. However, crime still thrives under conditions of affluence, and it is the white collar economic crime which erodes the capitalist system and which promotes more controls and less freedom, as can be observed day by day. In brief, the police, courts and prisons alone cannot control crime. We must also deal with the underlying cause of crime. The immense and stubborn forces pervading our environment determine the quality of our lives and are a challenge to us.
Through long range efforts in a new land of bountiful resources we can conquer poverty, ignorance, disease, discrimination, family breakdown, injustice, social tension, and despair. But while we must strive to approach the causes of crime, we must put our mind to work in a practical way to amend the various sections of the Criminal Code to guarantee that the law is respected and is not shaped and planned so as to protect the rich only and be unjust toward the poor. Crime is a national problem under our constitution, while law enforcement is the provincial and local responsibility. This parliament must direct its processes so as to ensure justice through the Criminal Code. It is for us to bring excellence to every aspect of the administration of justice-to corrections, the courts, and to law enactment in every jurisdiction in Canada.
Let me turn my attention now to the administration of justice. I was disappointed to see that two bills, Bill C-51 and Bill C-52, which were brought forward by the former minister of justice, died on the order paper. Bill C-52 contained the new definition of rape and indecent assault or aggravated indecent assault. Although I cannot say I agree with all the clauses of the bill, I think that the purpose of the bill was good. The purpose of the bill was to correct the procedures of the courts which sometimes allow the victim to suffer more than the accused, and cross-examination procedures which allow the victims to be cross-examined on their past sexual behaviour.
The Council on the Status of Women for Canada met with our committee and with the caucus of our party and discussed that very problem. One of the things they asked was that this parliament take steps to assist victims of rape, a crime which is on the increase in this nation, particularly in the highrises, on parking lots, and in the streets and alleys.
Bill C-51 was a large, omnibus bill. Our all-party committee on justice and legal affairs met to study the question of pornography, and for once members from all parties agreed to a report, because as pornography is defined in the Criminal

October 17, 1978
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
Code under section 159(1) at the present time there have been few convictions. The problem was the meaning of the definition on obscene written matter and whether it met community standards, because the standards of one community can differ from that of another. I could deal with facts in some of those cases in which there were commitals. There are pictures showing the greatest kind of perversion of mankind, but I do not want to get into that.
The point I wish to emphasize is that the definition of pornography under the Criminal Code as it exists is inadequate and does not serve society. If there is a problem I get more letters on, it is the problem of pornography across this nation. It arises in part in the local corner store where young children can go in, sit down and read or see the weirdest kind of pornography dealing with both mature adults and children as young as two and three years of age. One distributor admitted that he made over $1 million in the maritime provinces alone in selling and peddling pornography. He could not tell us what amount was made across Canada because he did not have the figures.
Under that bill we were able to convince the Minister of Justice to change the definition of pornography. Under that bill section 159(8) in the Code was to be repealed. It was defined as follows:
A dominant characteristic of the matter or thing is the undue exploitation of sex, violence, crime, horror, cruelty or the undue degradation of the human person; or
(b) the matter or thing unduly depicts a totally or partially nude child
(i)	engaged or participating in an act or a simulated act of masturbation, sexual intercourse, gross indecency, buggery or bestiality, or
(ii)	unduly displaying any portion of his or her body in a sexually suggestive manner.
That bill died on the order paper. It would seem that this government has now forgotten its mandate, which it thought it had, on reform.
In dealing with the Criminal Code we have referred to the expertise of the Law Commission. It has been sitting for a number of years, and I was very pleased to see Mr. Francis C. Muldoon, QC, a member of the Manitoba Bar, take over the chairmanship. He came before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and I spoke to him. I said that for a number of years the Law Reform Commission has done an excellent job but they have been philosophizing. Every report they put out is philosophical and I felt that it was time they, in spending the $2.5 million of the taxpayers' money they receive for this year, came to grips with some of the amendments in the Criminal Code.
One of the matters which should be looked at is the definition of insanity which determines whether a person is insane or not. This law was written over 100 years ago and is known as the M'Naghten rules. A person is said to be insane if he or she does not know (a) the nature and quality of their act, or (b), if the act is wrong. Surely that should be reviewed in light of new knowledge in psychology and psychiatry.
Section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act should be repealed and a new subsection enacted to empower a judge of the

Federal Court or other superior court to decide whether documents should be admitted as evidence in a court of law rather than leaving the matter to be determined by a minister of the Crown. This section has been used in reference to the McDonald inquiry. However, now the government has decided that it will determine what documents this national inquiry will see, that it will make the decisions and keep the facts from this inquiry. How can the inquiry come out with a report that is looking into wrongdoing? We do not know today, particularly when we talk about Section 41(2), what instructions were given by the many solicitors general that have come and gone. In fact they come and go as often as I wear out overcoats.
Laws must be examined, and enacted if necessary, to preserve always the jury trial system in Canada. There is a suggestion from the Law Reform Commission that we do away with juries. In all important cases I believe that every Canadian should have the right to be tried by his peers, and I would not want any other system to develop in this country in our jurisprudence. There has been some recommendation also in reference to the abolition of preliminary hearings in criminal offences. Preliminary hearings must always be preserved in reference to charges under the Criminal Code dealing with serious crimes such as murder, rape or robbery, because it gives the accused's counsel a chance to determine what the Crown has in evidence so that he or she may properly prepare their defence. This eliminates the risk of mistakes, and there are mistakes made.
Divorces are far too costly. The law regarding grounds should be extended and therefore amended to streamline the procedure which will cut the cost to the average person.
All writs of assistance must be renewed every six months by a judge's order, not issued by some bureaucrat or official, to carry any legal force and effect.
I would like now to turn my attention to something which amounts to a complete abuse of law and the fundamental principles of jurisprudence. Parliament in its wisdom-some would question that-enacted legislation to abolish capital punishment. I am not here to discuss the question of capital punishment, I am here to tell the government and the Department of Justice that what they did when they changed the definition of murder and the procedure in dealing with this crime usurps the civil rights of those people charged with the offence under the old definition.
In bringing forth this legislation they changed the definition for the crime of murder. Formerly, murder was described as capital murder and non-capital murder, and it was changed to first degree and second degree murder. In comparing capital murder and first degree murder there is no difference in definition, and the same is true for non-capital murder and second degree murder. The legislation that was approved by this House was described as transitional and came into effect on July 16, 1976, and was to apply to deeds previously committed. Putting it simply, if a person committed an act on Monday and the new law is enacted in reference to the same crime on Friday, how can that person be asked to be a law-abiding citizen?
October 17, 1978

With this new section a person could be committed for trial under the old act, tried and convicted before July 16, 1976, then appeal his case and take it to the court of appeal where it is heard after the new legislation has been enacted. There are three cases that I am aware of like this, two of which I will name, the Pineault case of Ontario and the Budic case of Alberta. The third one is presently before the courts, and I will not mention it because I do not wish to deal with something now before the courts in reference to this question. All three individuals received new trials.
The trap was sprung. Section 27(2) of the Criminal Code which was approved by this House-I was a member at the time but I do not think anyone thought it would be used this way-reads as follows:
Where proceedings in respect of any offence of treason, piracy or murder, whether punishable by death or not, were commenced before the coming into force of this act, and a new trial of a person for the offence has been ordered and the new trial is commenced after the coming into force of this act, the new trial shall be commenced by the preferring of a new indictment-
What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? When a person committed an offence before the law was enacted by parliament, he was tried under the old law and found guilty under the old law. The court of appeal directed that the conviction be quashed and a new trial ordered. Then the Crown comes along-when the person has been charged with non-capital murder and is successful in the appeal-and prefers an indictment of first degree murder. This is retroactive legislation of the worst kind and is against all the principles for which jurisprudence ever stood.
I have already referred to Regina vs-. Pineault (1977) 32 CCR, page 391, Court of Appeal of Ontario. I will skip the next one because I know something about it, and it is before the courts. The next one is Regina vs. Budic. The Court of Appeal of Ontario split two to one on the interpretation. It does not say an indictment under the old act or under the new act, and that has never been settled by the Supreme Court of Canada. If you do a deed, no matter how evil, and it is on Monday, surely this parliament in its wisdom should not pass an act on Friday and make it retroactive to what you did on Monday. If that is the law of the land, God help the citizens of this country. This is legislation drafted by this government, brought in by this government, rammed through by this government which is now running slip-shod over people who get new trials in the court of appeal.
The following statement by Mr. Justice Brooks, a dissenting judge in the Pineault case, is the most serious I have read in the administration of justice for many years. He said:
Having regard to the whole of s. 27 of the act, it seems clear that parliament set a cut-off date. It said that after the coming into force of the act all charges of murder would proceed as murder in the first degree or murder in the second degree and an accused not yet tried and one for whom a new trial had been ordered by an appellate court would accordingly be similarly treated. To this extent parliament has declared what is fair and just. However, the important distinction (and really it is a safeguard) is that where a new trial has been ordered the appellate court was under a duty when directing the new trial to make any order that Justice requires. It is the presence of this obligation that is perhaps an answer to Mr. Greenspan's submission that his man's successful
Business of the House
exercise of his right of appeal from his conviction for non-capital murder is no more than a sham.
In other words, if a person appeals to the court of appeal on a serious charge of non-capital murder and obtains a new trial, he is in worse shape than had he never appealed at all, even if there is a mistake in law or a mistake in evidence. That is what we call retroactive law. This has not reached the Supreme Court of Canada. There may not be many cases on the point.
Another change in the Criminal Code is that you can only appeal from a conviction or acquittal, so that means you cannot go to the Supreme Court of Canada on a motion. Mr. Justice Brooks also said:
Having regard to what has happened in this case and for the reasons which I have stated, I think the court should act and direct that the new trial be upon an indictment which charges the appellant with second degree murder and I would so order.
However, the other two judges decided the other way. So I say that for a person who committed an evil act before this legislation became law, if he is successful in appeal, the retroactive legislation means he finds himself charged on an indictment of first degree murder, rather than second degree murder as punishment for winning his appeal. If that is the law of Canada, I do not even want to be an honorary pallbearer at its funeral.
Mr. Driedger, the director of legislation for the federal government, has said:
A retroactive statute is one that operates as of a time prior to its enactment. A retrospective statute is one that operates for the future only. It is prospective but it imposes new results in respect of a past event.
He goes on to say that retroactive legislation should never apply to criminal matters. If there is any ambiguity, it should lean toward the citizen rather than the state.
Finally, this new law, in the guise of abolishing capital punishment, appears to have changed the whole process of the fundamental principle of justice, that a person must know the law as he sits, as he walks, as he runs, and as he acts, not some law that comes into force after the fact. I ask the House to take a hard look at that.
I want to deal with one more thought, if I have time, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I believe it is appropriate to say, if at first you do not succeed try, try, try again. First of all I would like to congratulate the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) as mover, and the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Savard) as seconder of the motion, both of whom spoke with compassion and clarity. I was very proud to have them as members of the House and members of my party.
The events of last night and the clear knowledge that we are facing an election within the next few months are very evident to all of us. I would like to say at the beginning of my comments that, be that as it may, this parliament must work in the meantime. 1 want to speak this afternoon with what I feel will be considerable candour. As my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), stated we will be having a budget in November. Today I would like to place before the House some facts on the fiscal position of the government so that we may all, in our responsibilities as parliamentarians representing whatever party, have that knowledge when we consider what might or might not be done three or four weeks from now, and indeed from now until the spring, in meeting our responsibilities collectively for the Canadians we represent.
1 was tempted to divert from those comments, but I will not go too far, by the incident that took place when I tried to speak previously, when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) made some comments before the end of his remarks.

I would like to say that there was some outrage felt here about the personal comments concerning the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), which I think were taken out of context and which were registered by my colleague, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald). I will deal with another comment which the right hon. member made and which I do not feel is personally outrageous, but incorrect, when he stated that the borrowings of the government last year were $13 billion, I believe he said, when in fact they were $7 billion. As well he forecast $15 to $16 billion in borrowings this year. Instead they will be $11.8 billion. speechtext:
I will resist the temptation of further diversion because in the time that is available 1 want to set forth some views and some facts that I have. The economic problems we face are international in scope. Governments all over the world are grappling with inflation, with unemployment, with trade problems, and with currency difficulties.
No industrial nation that I know of is isolated from the other industrial nations, and indeed nor is Canada. Objectively we are doing better than most, but Canadians are concerned and we are concerned. We are concerned as a government, and as members of parliament, about the persistent and pervasive nature of continuing inflation, unemployment, growth below our potential, and currency devaluation; we know the litany.
These days it seems economic theories that were well accepted are being challenged, be they Keynes or even our old friend Adam Smith, Freidman, Samuelson or whoever. It is my experience that if there are ten economists in the room, eleven different ideas of what should be done will be voiced. Governments in Canada of all stripes and at all levels since the 1960s have been intervening increasingly in the private sector. We see more spending, and more regulations. The growth of government in many people's view has begun to encroach, psychologically if not substantively, and it has begun to stifle the initiative of the private sector. The curious thing is that even with this growth in spending of governments, hon. members should know from their analysis and research that tax revenues have not kept pace with spending. This government is not alone in that case. Government spending at all levels in Canada, federal, provincial and municipal, is on the same scale.
In 1961, about 15 or 16 years ago, collectively in our various administrations we took about 31 per cent and spent about 31 per cent of the gross national product. By 1976 in Canada that figure had reached 40.3 per cent, an increase of 9.5 per cent, of the economy going through government hands, federal, provincial and municipal. The federal government, including the transfer payments to the provinces, accounted for 2.1 per cent of that 9.5 per cent. And the other levels of government,
The Address-Mr. Andras
even before the effect of transfers to them, actually spent the money and accounted for 7.4 per cent.
If you exclude the transfer payments to the provincial governments, that money we collected through the federal tax revenue system and sent by way of cheques to the provincial governments, our share of that 9.5 per cent increase in the GNP was 0.5 per cent their's was 9 per cent. I do not say that as a criticism of the provincial and municipal governments. Indeed, let us be honest about it. Some of these programs for which we transferred funds were initiated at the federal level, medical and that kind of thing. Nevertheless we have to put the facts before us, and hopefully before Canadians as they judge this question of taxation and spending. It is important to know where that distribution is. It is also interesting in terms of the arguments of centralization and decentralization in this country.
That is where the spending increase took place in the main, at the provincial and municipal levels. And incidentally those seem like small percentages, that 0.5. I often hear that our expenditures have gone from $16 billion to $50 billion-"Isn't that shocking"? and "Indeed that is startling." But nobody adds to that that next year the gross national product of this country will be $250 billion. It has to have a form of relativity, one to the other. It is the standard, internationally speaking, by which government expenditures are judged. That is the relative position vis-a-vis the national economy. It is not the only criteria by which spending should be judged, by any stroke of the imagination. Efficiency, effectiveness and value for money are very good things. But in the macroeconomic effect of it that is the standard by which internationally, governments are judged in terms of their spending.
Even with that increase to which I have referred, which in my view was too much and too rapid, we are still in the low quarter of western industrialized countries as to the degree of public spending. I am talking about governments collectively. At any rate we have certainly contributed, as a federal government and in this House too, in my view and that of many others, to too rapid a growth.
It took place in the main in the period 1972 to 1975, a very responsive and quite expensive period of minority government. We were increasing our spending year by year at a rate which was clearly unsustainable. However, in 1976, and the facts are there, we changed course. We made a public commitment to reduce the growth of our spending to something below the growth in our economy, the gross national product.
I am talking about spending including transfer payments to the provinces, to people, budgetary, non-budgetary, capital, non-capital spending, the total over-all cash flow of the government. We met that commitment in 1976, 1977 and 1978, and we will meet it in 1979.

October 17, 1978
The Address-Mr. Andras
Spending by governments and taxation by governments is of concern to the populace. Proposition 13 in California is not as alien or foreign as it may be considered by virtue of not being in this country.
More recently, spending in Canada by governments received more attention by virtue of the fact that in August we announced certain steps to cut our expenditures more significantly than we had up until then. I am quite aware of the cynicism as to, first of all, is it the right policy. I know that the New Democratic Party, I think in sincerity, might challenge as to whether it is or is not. Others challenge it through general cynicism.
I know there is cynicism as to whether the cuts are real or not. In the few minutes left to me I would like to establish why I and my colleagues believe it is the right policy and is necessary. I hope we will not have to waste a lot more time as to whether the cuts are real or not. I do not think the people in Ottawa have much doubt about that.
That was not a recent conversion on the road to Damascus. It began as a policy stated, followed through, committed and met in 1976. Granted, on August 1 it escalated and took on considerably more significance. About two or three years ago in a white paper called "The Way Ahead" we said that we had come to the conclusion that it was time the government backed off a little from the private sector, stopped stifling them and began giving them more room.
We had a series of ex-budgets and cuts, three or four which I, as President of the Treasury Board during my regime, had to administer, and a couple that my predecessor, the Minister of Finance, had to administer. I grant you that in those times and at those stages we were trying to make those reductions and that restraint as painless as possible. It is not a natural instinctive desire on the part of governments to cut back. None of us came to parliament simply to balance books. We all came to try and do something.
In our wisdom in those days, we put programs together which we thought were right. Collectively, I am afraid, they added up to an overkill and so we had to cut back. We were doing it as painlessly as possible.
On April 1 of this year, the April problem I call it, my people did a tally for me about the inexorable and inevitable growth of spending for next year. As I said publicly, my hair went white. It was far too high. It would have broken through the commitment to stay within the GNP trend line. Something significant had to be done.
We began right away, with full concurrence of my cabinet colleagues, to begin the cutbacks. They were larger than in the past. We had achieved a fair amount of that by the time the August 1 date came along. However, it was slow, painful, and somewhat tenuous as to whether we were going to get that last few hundred million we figured we needed to get to certain ceilings we had agreed to at that stage, ceilings which I felt at that time were still too high.
The Prime Minister returned from Bonn, having had the opportunity to talk with leaders of other countries, probably in

private, commiserating on similar problems, saying what in the devil do we do about this? They talked frankly with each other away from the glare of the television spotlight, away from newspaper reporters and everybody else. There were discussions.
When the Prime Minister returned, he called me and said that we had to go further than we had planned. I subscribed to that position. He made it public that we were going to fulfil our commitment, that we were going to get our spending levels in line as we publicly committed in August. Indeed, our objective at that time was to go even further, because to get to lower spending ceilings was not enough. It did not give us one dime to reroute, reorder and put into new and more required initiatives of the current needs of this country, funding for new programs that we thought were necessary. Therefore we went further and rerouted another billion or so dollars back into the system in certain ways.
We took $500 million off this year to cut our ceiling to $48,300 million. We have taken $2 billion off for next year to get from $54,600 million to $52,600 million.
I have talked about inexorable growth, the inevitable spending levels that would have hit us. People say we are setting up a straw figure of $54,600 million simply to knock down, so that we can say we cut it. Not so. We have built into federal spending some inevitable growth pressures by law and federal-provincial contract.
Let me describe spending in four main areas. We have hundreds of programs. We cut or modified 189. I refer to transfer payments, transfers to persons, UIC, old age security, family allowance and the like, as well as transfers to the provinces, established program financing, equalization payments, post-secondary education, medical care and that kind of thing.
Those are the programs that are growing. Those are the programs that have absolutely the highest degree of commitment that parliament can give. As we know, our social programs, transfers to persons, are by law indexed to the cost of living. That is the least of the escalation formulas.
Many of our contractual obligations to the provinces are contractually committed to growth escalation formulae, the nominal growth of the gross national product which includes real growth and inflation. Socially, that may be right or that may be wrong. However, it is very, very expensive, and it is there as a commitment.
Let me give a sense of the degree in terms of the $52,600 million ceiling next year. Half of it, $26 billion, will be in transfer payments. The over-all annual growth rate of the transfer payment portion of our expenditures, where we collect taxes and send cheques, is around 10 per cent. It varies from about 9.8 per cent to 11 per cent on some of them. That huge portion of our expenditures carries with it legislative or contractual commitment to escalation formulas.
You cannot cut those back unilaterally. They take legislative amendment and we are going to propose some of those, or they take negotiations with the provinces and we have indicated to
October 17, 1978

the provinces that we must sit down together and jointly try to get this thing in line, not vindictively I hope but practically for this country. We hope they will see, as we see, that it is time to make some of these adjustments.
I now come to the servicing of the public debt. Anybody who blithely says today, "Spend more", or "Consider tax cuts", had better clearly understand thay every dime of that will be borrowed money. I regret the statements by the right hon. member for Prince Albert and his leader over the last little while about the $16 billion deficit. It is not true and, in my view, is damaging. Nevertheless, $11.7 billion is not peanuts, and interest on that has to be paid. We are going to have a $9.7 billion cash requirement next year even with the lower ceilings.
In 1973 we indexed taxation downwards; revenue is indexed downwards and expenditures are indexed upwards. Thus we were accumulating deficits over the past few years in a Keynesian application which, in my view, is no longer working. So when we talk next year, or when we get to budget time, about stimulating the economy, let us together as parliamentarians face this one fact, and make our decisions with this one fact before us, that we are borrowing money at interest rates which, as we know, are currently high, and that more of that borrowing is in the 20-year markets. So it is our children and grandchildren we are talking about, and that public debt service cost is accounting for more and more of our gross expenditures. So we are being squeezed. Hon. members should bear this in mind when we, as parliamentarians of any party, consider what should be done in the area of stimulation by the federal government one way or another.
I also want to say that the end-effectiveness is probably unsustainable at some stage in the kind of expenditure cuts we are making. I have had the painful and difficult task of assuming some responsibility for the $2 billion cuts scheduled for next year and the $500 million for this year, in addition to other cuts we have made. I tell you frankly, Mr. Speaker, that because of the nature of the commitments under transfer payments and because of the inevitability of debt repayment, unless we are to go bankrupt these cuts can only be made at the expense of the direct operations of the federal government in the field of transportation and so on which come clearly under federal jurisdiction.
Next year, out of the $4.3 billion increase in spending, something like $2.5 billion will be in the transfer payments and around $1.5 billion in the interest charges. I invite hon. members to do a little arithmetic and see how much room there is left for an increase in the operations of the federal government itself, or even for the maintenance of direct federal programs. Only 0.8 per cent of the increase in our spending next year will be spent in the direct operations of the federal government itself. If we go on for three or four or five years- and I believe in the maintenance of reasonable ceilings-we cannot continue to take it out of our own hide or we shall end up as a cheque-writing institution just sending cheques to the
The Address-Mr. Andras
social programs, which are fine in principle, and to the provinces.
These observations should be taken into account by all of us, I say so candidly, as in the remaining days of this parliament we try to come to grips, apart from our adversary roles, with what can be done. Is adherence to some kind of ceiling sound, or should we go on and on? Well, Mr. Speaker, we cannot go spending or cutting taxes in that sense and borrowing money because we are mortgaging the future of a lot of people, not just ourselves but those who come after us.

speechtext: What about the private sector?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Well, I know it is said, often sincerely, that we should increase public spending. I am not worried about the ideological label attached to it but I do not think it would work. I do not think governments are that good at doing things. There is no question the private sector has got to get off its butt and start doing things. But we have to give it the necessary encouragement and the stimulation.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board

speechtext:
I have a quotation here, if I can find it, which I thought was pretty apt. The retiring managing director of the International Monetary Fund-his name is Witteveen- summed up my feelings on the matter. He said:
I do not think that I have had to change my economic views in any major way. Perhaps I have seen more clearly, as have a number of economists and politicians, that in many situations it may no longer be possible to increase employment by more government spending. To get a more healthy growth it may-even be necessary to reduce government spending and to give more room to the private sector.
That is, I think, a feature that we have seen in a number of member countries, and at first sight it might seem to be a contradiction of Keynesian prescriptions. In reality, I think it is not. In the mixed economy, the private sector needs sufficient room to live, and to breathe, and to grow. That is a lesson that I have seen clearly.
That statement comes from a man who was in an excellent position to judge. I do not think this is an ideological argument. I think it is a practical argument. So I place these views before hon. members. There is going to be an $11.7 billion cash borrowing this year and, subject only to the possible fluctuation of revenue, $9.7 billion next year-not the larger requirements or deficits which have been touted about, but still sizeable. So, as we deliberate about what the economic stance of the federal government should or should not be in terms of stimulation, let us be very sure we know the consequences of that stimulation in the long term.

speechtext:
that Bill C-8, to provide for the resumption and continuation of postal services, be read the second time and referred to the committee of the whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my first words must be to place on record how regrettable I find it to take the time of this House to request that parliament bring an end to a labour-management dispute. It should not be necessary for me to reiterate the faith both this government and my predecessors in the Labour portfolio have in the free collective bargaining process. Canada's industrial relations system reflects our heritage which rests on fundamental western values and on our belief that the workers' well-being can best be promoted through free collective bargaining and the constructive settlement of disputes in a spirit of compromise.
The state has assumed the task of establishing a framework of rights and responsibilities in which management and organized labour are to conduct their relations. That framework places the responsibility for resolving labour-management disputes clearly on the parties to collective bargaining. Hon. members will recall recent examples where this responsibility has been fulfilled by parties to labour-management disputes involving the public interest. I have in mind the three separate disputes between Air Canada and representatives of its ground personnel, its pilots, and its flight attendants. I also have very much in mind the recent negotiated settlement, with mediation assistance, between the Letter Carriers Union of Canada and the Treasury Board.
Unfortunately, however, there are times and situations when the spirit of compromise and the demonstration of good faith, so necessary on the part of all concerned, are found wanting. In such circumstances the federal government, as custodian of the economy and protector of the public interest, must assume its responsibility. This is the case at the present time in the dispute between the Post Office and the Canadian Union of Postal Workers. Parliament must, unfortunately, be resorted to today if we are to bring to an end a situation which the public finds intolerable. Parliament must legislate an end to this dispute if we are to take seriously into account the public interest and the extent to which the citizens of this country will continue to be affected by a prolonged stoppage of postal services.
It might be useful if I were to review the sequence of events which has led to this stage, and to remind hon. members of the extended efforts employed over many months to resolve the dispute.
It is clear from a review of developments leading up to the present impasse between the inside postal workers and management that there has been a complete lack of meaningful communication and dialogue between the parties and almost no real bargaining; that is, the necessary compromises and counter-proposals on which a viable collective agreement and bargaining relationship can be based have been completely absent.
Without attempting to cast blame on one party or the other, it would be useful to set out some of the important events in the present dispute.
The previous collective agreement between CUPW and the Treasury Board expired on June 30, 1977.
In the early months of 1977 several pre-negotiation meetings took place between the parties, without any progress being made.
On May 4, 1977, the union served formal notice to bargain, with Treasury Board replying on May 6, 1977.
The first formal meeting, which took place on May 19,
1977,	lasted one hour and was the only one for several months.
Negotiations were finally held again in October and November. However, little progress was made.
On November 30, 1977, the employer filed an application with the Public Service Staff Relations Board for the appointment of a conciliation board. Mr. Roy Heenan, on behalf of management, and Mr. Irving Gaul, on behalf of the union, were named to the conciliation board on December 17, 1977. Mr. Louis Courtemanche was appointed chairman of the board on February 2, 1978.
There were many public conciliation hearings from April through to July, 1978. Closed conciliation sessions involving both parties began in the early part of July and continued through to the end of the month. During these extensive conciliation board proceedings, the parties were able to agree to only a few minor clauses.
On August 16, 1978, the union gave notice that it wished the conciliation process to terminate and asked the board to prepare its report.
The conciliation board handed down three separate reports, which were released to the parties on October 6, 1978. The lack of agreement among the three members of the conciliation board is an indication of the intense feelings of the parties and the wide differences between them on a very large number of complex contract items. Notwithstanding the very exhaustive efforts of the conciliation board from April to August
1978,	little was achieved in bringing the parties closer to agreement, and since the handing down of the three separate board reports it is apparent that very wide gaps between the parties still exist.
Hon. members will have learned that yesterday I and senior officials of the Department of Labour made what is called a last ditch effort to resolve this dispute in a spirit of conciliation and compromise when we met twice yesterday with representatives of the union, along with a representative of the Canadian
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
October 17, 1978

Labour Congress, in order to explore all possible avenues leading to a settlement.
Following intense exploratory talks I proposed two possible means of resolving the dispute, which were given to the parties for their consideration. The first proposal called for the application of the mediation-arbitration process, "med-arb" as it is called in labour jargon, in the resolution of this dispute.
This process has been used successfully in other cases, not too long ago with the longshoremen at the port of Montreal, and also not too long ago on three different occasions with grain handlers in western Canada. This process involves agreement by the parties to refer their dispute to a mediator-arbitrator who would seek to mediate all outstanding issues originally referred by the Public Service Staff Relations Board to the conciliation board chaired by Mr. Courtemanche. This process would also require the parties to agree further that the mediator, should he not be successful in mediating the whole of the collective agreement, would then make an arbitration finding on all remaining unresolved issues. The parties would agree to be bound by the arbitration awards rendered. In this process the mediator would be appointed by the Minister of Labour and would submit his report to the parties not later than 90 days following the date of his appointment.
The second proposal put forward by myself for consideration by the parties would require that the employer and CUPW return to the bargaining table with full authority to settle all issues in dispute, under the auspices of a special commissioner appointed by myself to mediate the dispute.
The issues to be dealt with would be those that were referred by the Public Service Staff Relations Board to the conciliation board chaired by Mr. Courtemanche. The commissioner would be required to attempt a resolution of all such issues within two weeks of his appointment. If, at the end of the two-week period, any issues remained unresolved, the commissioner would then report to myself stating, in his opinion, what further steps or procedures would be required to finalize an agreement.
Both of these proposals which were presented to the parties yesterday evening included the stipulation that during either of the processes, if accepted by the parties, the government would put aside its intention to bring in legislation, and the union would agree to withhold any strike authorization and to direct its members to return to work. Such conditions are necessary to allow mediation to take place in a spirit of good faith and without threat on either side. I must say that it is regrettable that the union felt its objective would be best accomplished under the duress of a strike.
Unfortunately, the national executive board for the union rejected both of our proposals for the resolution of this dispute and called a national strike last night. Needless to say, I am very disappointed in the national executive board's reaction, as we have made every possible effort to resolve this dispute through a negotiated settlement in the spirit of conciliation and compromise.
Postal Services
There appear now to be only two courses left open to the government: either to allow the strike to continue with no hope of settlement available to the parties in the foreseeable future, or to legislate an end to the work stoppage and bring about a resumption of postal operations while providing for a resolution of the dispute.
We have opted for the second resolution because we have exhausted, over a protracted period of time, all statutory procedures under the Public Service Staff Relations Board, together with all good offices, including those of the Department of Labour, to resolve the dispute, and because we have failed to convince the union to accept either of the proposals for the resolution of the dispute which I presented to them yesterday evening.
It is the fundamental belief of this government that when an individual right becomes a public wrong, parliament should terminate the dispute. It is in keeping with this philosophy that this urgent matter is now before you.
This act, to provide for the resumption and continuation of the postal service, orders, therefore, the immediate resumption of the postal services, and provides for a determination of a collective agreement between the Canadian Union of Postal Workers and the Treasury Board of Canada relative to the Canada Post Office.
The bill calls for the appointment by the Minister of Labour of a person who will deploy every effort to mediate the outstanding issues originally referred by the Public Service Staff Relations Board to the conciliation board chaired by Mr. Courtemanche. Should there be items that cannot be mutually agreed to in this mediation process, the bill provides that this mediator will then make an arbitration finding on all remaining unresolved issues. His award on these items will be binding on both parties concerned, and will be rendered not later than 90 days following the date of his appointment.
In its final report to parliament, the Special Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service stated the following in respect of prosecutions under the Public Service Staff Relations Act:
The present two-stage process with its substantial costs, delays, fragmented administration, absence of precedents, and inconsistent penalties has led all parties to agree that the present system for dealing with unlawful activity is not working well and is inappropriate.
The government has indicated on previous occasions that it will be bringing forward comprehensive amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act which will include a response to the recommendations of the joint committee concerning prosecutions and penalties for unlawful activity.
It is important, however, that the bill with which we are dealing now be not frustrated in its application by the enforcement deficiencies of the Public Service Staff Relations Act which were recognized by the joint committee. The government, therefore, proposes that the intent of the joint committee's proposals on prosecution for unlawful activity be incorporated into this act.
80065 -13'/2

October 17, 1978
Postal Services
In particular, clause 10 of the bill includes penalties which directly follow those recommended by the joint committee. The joint committee also envisaged a single stage process whereby prosecutions would be brought before the Public Service Staff Relations Board. Since it would not be feasible to set up exactly this process in the short time required, the government is proposing that a single stage process be provided by eliminating the necessity for consent to prosecute offences under this act.
Hon. members will note that the bill provides for a term extending to 1979. The main reason for that is to prevent an early occurrence of the present situation and to ensure an uninterrupted postal service during the transition period of the planned conversion of the Post Office to a Crown corporation. We believe that is necessary in order to effect a good transition without impairing the efficiency of the Crown corporation.

Mr. Speaker, the government faces two alternatives: it can let this strike go on without any hope that the parties will come to an agreement in the near future, or it can legislate to end this work stoppage, thereby ensuring the resumption of postal services and a settlement of the dispute.
We have, of course, chosen the second alternative, after having exhausted during a lengthy period of negotiations all procedures provided for by the Public Service Staff Relations Board as well as all other means, including the intervention of the Department of Labour, and also because we have been unable to convince the union to accept either one of the two offers I submitted to them yesterday in an attempt to arrive at a negotiated settlement of this dispute. The government staunchly believes that public interest must override personal interest and that it is up to parliament to implement this philosophy. That is why this vital question is before the House today.

In closing I would like to say that I sincerely hope that the parties will take advantage of this interim period to re-establish a climate of confidence conducive to improving labour-management relations and leading to the restoration of the high calibre of postal service of which this country has been rightly proud in the past.
With these explanations, Mr. Speaker, and in full realization of the seriousness of the situation which confronts us all, I trust the House will give full and speedy approval to this legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising on behalf of my party to respond to the words of the minister, I want to make several things clear at the outset. The first is that while we too regret the necessity for the legislation which is put before us, we will support it and we will not delay the passage of this law unduly, because it is our opinion that at this time the country cannot afford, not just the inconvenience, but the gravest damage which it will suffer in the case of a prolonged cessation of postal services.

[ Translation]
The Canadian economy, shaky as it is, cannot sustain an extended postal strike. Financial losses would be enormous and totally unacceptable. It would impose great and undue hardships on those people whose monthly cheque, sent to them by mail, is the only means they have of making both ends meet.
Mr. Speaker, our position is quite clear; this legislation must be passed immediately.
It is also important to point out that, while our position is clear, the position of the government is hard to comprehend. We had a postal strike just a few years ago, and this government, through the minister responsible for maintaining postal service, allowed service to end for a period of 43 days. During that time the then postmaster general said that he did not mind if it went on until Christmas, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated that he did not mind if it went on until Easter. I point this out because something-and it is not for me to say what it is-has certainly brought about an amazing difference in view on the part of the government as to the value of postal service in this vast land of ours.
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I would remind the minister- and I know that he would not mind being reminded-that my leader on October 6, 1978, called for the government to act swiftly and indicated then our full co-operation, provided of course the bill was essentially a fair bill, even though we would prefer to have the matter solved in some other way. Again on Friday, October 13, the House leader of my party reiterated our determination to co-operate and to move swiftly in the public interest, and that of course is what we are doing.
Parliament has been called to end strikes twice in 1972, 1973, 1974, 1975, 1976, and a special bill was passed in 1977. In some instances it was not a long or difficult debate, but each time that this has happened the government has said that this does not mean that we do not agree with the right of free collective bargaining and that it has always deplored the necessity to do this. The response of our party has been that there must be a better way.
It will be of interest to all hon. members to note that on August 31, 1973, when there was the long debate in this chamber as a consequence of the rail strike, my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), said, as reported at page 6175 of Hansard'.
Mr. Speaker, I merely want to say on behalf of our party that we hope this is the last time we are called upon to pass this type of legislation, because we feel there is a better way.
There is a better way, and it has been advocated by our party since the submission of the Woods Royal Commission on Canadian Industrial Relations, that there should be established a public interest disputes commission in order to reduce as much as possible the necessity of parliament interfering in these matters. There should be no doubt in anybody's mind that this has been our position, and I say this, in the hope of
October 17, 1978

solving the problem, to my friend the hon. minister, that we have maintained this position consistently for a number of years. In fact there has been favourable comment recently in labour circles that perhaps this recommendation by the Woods commission should be looked at further.
In closing, I would like to remind the House of what my colleague and friend, the hon. member for St. John's East, said on August 30, 1973, in this regard, as reported at page 6074 of Hansard:
Our party has put forward a proposal based on many of the recommendations contained in the Woods report. We have said we would establish an essential services disputes commission which would define essential services and prescribe the procedure for settling disputes within these essential services. Accordingly, our party endorsed the recommendations made to the government back in December, 1968, in the Woods committee report for the establishment of a public interest disputes commission. This commission would advise whether particular services are essential, set out procedures for resolving differences where the public interest is threatened and, where it is unsuccessful, would report to the government for possible parliamentary action to end a strike or lockout. That is the kind of leadership this country needs.
It has been my responsibility to speak on behalf of this party on a number of occasions when we have resorted to parliamentary measures to end strikes, and I am sure that hon. members will remember I have repeatedly stated that there must be a better way and that it is time, after these ten years and after the experiences which are there before us, to consider alternatives. I see the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet) sitting together. I am sure that they will agree that our experiences can lead us to only one conclusion, and that is that it is time to find, along the lines of the Woods commission, a better way.

subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Some years ago, Mr. Speaker, parliament passed the Public Service Staff Relations Act. If I remember correctly, it was passed almost unanimously. That act gave the public service employees working for the federal government the right to collective bargaining through unions of their choice, and it gave those unions two choices to settle their differences if they could not settle them through meetings with the employers and they were either through the process of arbitration or of taking strike action.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) mentioned earlier today that in more than 95 per cent of the cases the employees used the arbitration method to settle their differences with the government peaceably. The postal workers' union chose, as they had the right to do under the legislation, to avail themselves if necessary of the right to strike. I find it strange that this parliament and this government, having given workers in the public service the right to strike, is now asking parliament on the first day of the strike to take that right away from them.
There have been other occasions, both federally and provincially, where after a strike has gone on for some days or weeks the government, as represented at various times by all the political parties in Canada, has brought in legislation ordering the workers back to work because of the adverse effect of their strike on the public.
Postal Services
To my knowledge, this is the first time that legislation has been brought in to stop a strike on the day it began. If this government believes that this group of workers, or any other, is involved in operations so vital to the public of Canada that it ought not to have the right to strike, it seems to me it should have the courage to bring in that kind of legislation. We believe that in a democratic society all workers should have the right to strike. We would propose such legislation, but to give workers the right to strike and then take it away the first day they go on strike seems to us hypocritical to say the least.
If one did not live in Canada, one would have believed, listening to the minister, that this was an isolated case and that we had got along fine until now. One would think that we have a group of unreasonable people who, despite everything this generous government has done, and despite its human approach to its employees, are so unreasonable that they have gone on strike and the legislation is necessary. This is not an isolated case, Mr. Speaker. The difficulties in the Post Office have existed at least since 1965. I would remind the acting minister that after the 1965 strike the government established a royal commission of inquiry into working conditions in the Post Office. It was headed by Mr. Justice Montpetit, who made 262 recommendations dealing with all aspects of employment in the Post Office. Many of those recommendations still have not been implemented, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to read a couple of paragraphs from that report dealing with the attitude, not of the postal workers, but the attitude and approach of the management of the Post Office. The report reads:
A large number of the post office employees' grievances are first and foremost, human relations problems.
-The attitude of some supervisors and postmasters towards their employees leaves much to be desired. These people have only a vague notion of the importance of maintaining good relations with their staff.
The action of those in authority has and always will have a tremendous influence on the reactions of employees and on their productivity. Complaints arising from their behaviour can be sometimes difficult to explain.
Nothing much has changed since Mr. Justice Montpetit made that report in 1966. He pointed out that the Post Office Department did not have the authority to deal satisfactorily with its employees' requests because of the divided authority it had with the Civil Service Commission and the Treasury Board and certain other organizations. He certainly implied, if he did not say directly, that what we needed was probably a Crown corporation.
In 1968 a report was commissioned by the then postmaster general. It was entitled "A Blueprint for Change." I should like to put on the record part of what it said, as follows;
We believe that the Crown corporation status is the organizational form best suited to the attainment of these objectives.
These are the objectives of a good operation. The report went on to say:
As a Crown corporation, the Post Office should have full authority to bargain with the unions representing its employees. It should not be required to seek the approval of any government agency before concluding an agreement with unions.

October 17, 1978
Postal Services	_
With such freedom, a strong effective staff relations function would be required to guide management in its relationships with the unions.
That was ten years ago, Mr. Speaker, and the government did not act until a few weeks ago when it proposed to set up a Crown corporation.
I know that the minister will not deny that the Post Office and its senior officials have not been able to conduct negotiations with postal employees and that in effect the shots have been called by the Treasury Board which has been worried about the effect of a settlement achieved by postal workers on other employees.
For ten years this government has ignored the recommendations contained in a study made for it by a committee which it set up. Now it wonders why it is in trouble.
In 1969, in a dispute between postal workers and the Post Office Department, an adjudication decision was made by Mr. W. S. Martin, a well-known and competent person in that field. He said:
As assessment of employer attitudes in this matter shows that the employer position is characterized by arrogance and high-handedness. There is lacking a genuine desire to work in the atmosphere of mutual respect and understanding. Hostility, vindictiveness, and possibly distrust, appear to frustrate any opportunity for effective inter-relationships. It would appear that the senior officials in the Post Office Department have not as yet reconciled themselves to operating the postal facilities within a progressive collective bargaining atmosphere.
Nine years later the government has not learned anything.
A few years ago the union filed a grievance-they have filed between 30,000 and 60,000 grievances in all. This particular grievance was on behalf of a member, Alan O'Toole. It went through the grievance procedure provided in the collective agreement, and the union lost. Then they went to the adjudicator under the Public Service Staff Relations Act, and won. The employer did not accept that, and appealed to the Federal Court, where the union won. The Post Office did not accept that decision either, and filed an application to appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court rejected the application and refused to hear the case.
Mr. Speaker, that is not the way to conduct labour-management relations; it is not the spirit of trying to settle matters. That is the way to conduct things if you want to break the union by getting them involved in legal expenses they cannot afford.
In the dispute which took place in 1972 a conciliation board was involved. Mr. Justice Owen Shime was chairman. He said:
In these negotiations one felt that each time the employer was required to reach a decision that it was looking over its shoulder at the remaining government employees. That was an impediment to sound negotiations with respect to the needs and problems of the Post Office and its employees.
In 1975 the assistant deputy postmaster general, J. E. Uberig, submitted a report to the then postmaster general, Mr. Mackasey, in which he stated:
-although the Post Office Act states that the Postmaster General shall administer, superintend and manage the Post Office, the constraints imposed by other pieces of legislation acted to severely limit the ability of the Postmaster General to deal with problems. As a department of government, the Post Office has to conform to standards which, while applicable to other departments, serve
only to restrict the ability of Post Office management to deal with problems particular to postal operations.
He went on to be critical of the way the Public Staff Relations Act applied to the Post Office. Similarly, in a 1975 report prepared by the joint Post Office and Treasury Board committee, known as Canada Post '75, it was stated:
It was clear by 1975 that the program of regionalization begun in 1970 had been a dismal failure both financially and in respect to its impact on labour relations. Echoing a complaint of postal workers that regionalization had resulted in a destruction of a uniform criteria upon which disciplinary decisions were based, Canada Post 75 traced this unfortunate situation to the refusal of the government to implement the recommendations of A Blueprint For Change in their entirety.
A similar position was taken by the 1975 Conciliation Board headed by Judge Moisan.
The minister talked about what he had proposed to the postal union and suggested that they were not being very realistic and not considering his offer fairly. What the minister has failed to tell the House today is that for 18 months negotiations went on between CUPW and the government with no offer at all, no meaningful offer at all from the government. There was no offer on wages, nor on working conditions, technological change, staffing, or discipline, in fact, on nothing. It was the exact reverse, Mr. Speaker.
The government was proposing to take away from the workers the very important clause dealing with technological change which was negotiated in 1975. I think the minister knows, although he may not want to admit it, that the clause in the 1975 agreement dealing with technological change was imposed on the government and on the Treasury Board by the then postmaster general, Mr. Mackasey. As soon as Mr. Mackasey left that post the Treasury Board set out on a deliberate policy to sabotage and kill that provision of the contract. It is because of the insistence of the Treasury Board not to live up to clauses, such as the one concerning technological change, that thousands of grievances have been filed.
The whole question of technological change is not something which arose suddenly in the report. In 1966 Mr. Justice Montpetit made the following prophetic statement:
We should admit we were surprised that little mention was made of mechanization and automation by the postal clerks who will evidently be the first ones affected. Possibly they see this problem only far in the future. We believe this is a problem of prime importance which should be looked into immediately by all interested parties, since its effect will be very serious not only on job security but also on job classification, seniority, etc.
That was 1966, 12 years ago, and the government still has not faced up to the problem which Mr. Justice Monpetit said was so important. The government still has not accepted the basic principle that when an employer, government, or private enterprise, brings in technological change, it will mean that fewer workers will be needed, on that it should be done in such a way that workers at the time the technological change is brought into effect will not lose their jobs. It should be done on the basis of attrition.
[Mr. Orlikow.)
October 17, 1978

In 1969 Mr. W. S. Martin in his adjudication said:
It is quite clear that this conduct has resulted in creating unrest, the undermining of morale, and the development of hostility between the parties. Fairness and good faith must be in evidence to have a genuine willingness to consult. The autocratic issuance of directives and the unilateral determination of dates of implementation, do not provide requisites for the attainment of these results.
Let us take a simple illustration of how the Post Office management sees this whole question of technological change and classification. I am not a time study expert, and neither is the acting minister. I think he will agree with me that there is a vast difference between sorting mail by hand, as it was done for many years, and sorting mail through one of the new computerized operations in which thousands of letters flow through the machine every minute. There is no doubt in my mind that the highly automated operation is much harder physically and mentally on the worker than sorting mail by hand. And yet when the Post Office set the rate for the workers sorting mail automatically they set the rate at 75 cents less an hour than for those who were sorting by hand. Does the minister wonder why the workers in the Post Office are unhappy? Does he wonder why they do not have much faith in the Post Office or why they stopped work? They are completely frustrated.
In 1975 the agreement reached at that time spelled out the rights of employees with respect to the introduction of technological change. Clause 29, as I said earlier, was negotiated by the then minister, Mr. Mackasey. It has been constantly sabotaged by the government at the insistence of Treasury Board. The union filed a complaint which was heard by the vice chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, Mr. Jolliffe, who found for the union.
There has been real bargaining in good faith by the government. On the problems of technological change, of discipline, of staffing, of the use of casual employees, the government has failed to make any real offers or offers of significance in the months in which the negotiations were supposedly taking place. It was not until the workers had exhausted all their legal avenues, and had decided to set a strike date because they could not get anywhere without that weapon, that the minister entered the picture.
We are very unhappy that the negotiations conducted by the minister did not succeed. But I find it strange that there were more real negotiations in the last two or three days the minister entered the picture than in the 18 months before that.
