Why did they not meet with the employees and the union? Why did they not do what they should have done ten years ago and get rid of most of the senior officials of the Post Office Department who do not have the foggiest
Postal Services
notion of what real, sensible, honest collective bargaining means? That is what they should have done.
Because we believe there have been no real negotiations and because we believe the government has failed over a period of more than ten years to think through what is needed in order to improve the relationship between employee and the management of the post office, and that workers should have the right to strike-in which case they should not be legislated back to work on the first day or they do not have the right to strike in which case the legislation should say they do not-we cannot and will not vote for this bill.
I might say in conclusion that a brilliant job of public relations has been done by the senior officials of the Post Office so that the public has come to believe that the reason for the bad service and the delays is because the workers in the Post Office are not interested, because they are not working, because they are malingerers.
There may be a few workers in the Post Office, as I am sure there are a few workers in any organization, not putting out 100 per cent. However, I want to put on record my belief, based on the facts, I am certain, that the real difficulties in the Post Office, and the poor service people believe they are getting, are not the fault of the workers but of management. Let me put, in a very few papagraphs, what I mean.
Some ten years ago the senior people in the Post Office Department looked at the annual sharp increase in the amount of mail that was being handled. They decided that if they did not find some automated electronic way of handling mail to meet the increase, the number of people working for the Post Office would grow at a fantastic rate. A few of them travelled around the world looking at systems in other countries. When they returned, they persuaded this government that we needed the best system in the world.
The best system in the world is expensive. Therefore, we spent a billion dollars on new electronic equipment. That system is in operation, or should be in operation because it is in place, in Toronto. Through it moves 70 per cent of all the mail in Canada.
The computerized automated system is not working because all of its parts are not working. Some of those parts, including the computer system which costs between $150 million and $200 million, are still not working. The facilities in Toronto and Montreal are not functioning properly. The Montreal facility will not be finished until next year.
There are three plants in Toronto, the east plant in Scarborough, the south central plant, and the Gateway plant. Gateway has two plants, the west letter processing plant and the entry bulk mail facility. The second plant, the bulk mail facility at Gateway, is not working. This means that all mail arriving from Air Canada, from trains, from other cities in cartons and boxes and so on, is in trouble.
For example, all mail should go through Gateway, then on to other plants, but at Gateway's bulk mail facility section, the

October 17, 1978
Postal Services
mail handling computer does not work and the receiving pans did not line up mechanically properly. They are working on this second problem with some success, but there is no solution yet on the electronic computer problem. Its cost rose from %2Vi million to $7 million, yet the Post Office is not suing the company but absorbing the extra cost as developmental costs. I wish it would treat its employees as generously as it treats that company.
They had to vacate the old Terminal A. Now they are using the old arsenal building, and some other mail is being sorted in the letter processing plants which were not designed for this purpose. The result of these mistakes in planning is that all mail is moving slower than should be. Staff is inflated to handle the 50 per cent to 60 per cent of mail being sorted manually. Some mail is being semi-processed mechanically.
A lot of street letter mail does not have the code, or the code is not in the right place, not typed, or wrong letters and numbers have been used. This screws up the automatic system. The amount of mail being machine processed is lower than it is supposed to be or than the Post Office admits. The Post Office says it always expected to sort 27 per cent of the mail manually. The real amount being done that way is much higher. Therefore, they need extra help, I suppose the casual help about which there has been so much dispute.
Supposedly first class letters were to be processed mechanically, but this will not happen until the whole system is operating. Why did the Post Office let development time take so long? It will not be ready till next year at the earliest. Originally it was programmed to be ready last year.
Of these mistakes, let me say one thing. I hope the Postmaster General will correct me if I am wrong. I am told the system is operating so badly that mail which should be sorted in Toronto is being shipped to Cornwall where it is sorted and brought back to Toronto. That may not be true now, but I am told it has happened. If it is happening, those who should be in trouble are not the postal employees who belong to CUPW, but the postal management.
We were told in the Speech from the Throne that we are going to get a Crown corporation and this will solve all the problems. If it is run by the same people who have been running the Post Office for the past ten years, we will have more trouble with the Crown corporation than we have had up until now.
Let me conclude by saying that it is sad we have to discuss this kind of legislation. However, we have to discuss it because the government, postmasters general and presidents of the treasury board have been remiss in getting their act together. They have not worked out a policy for collective bargaining which is workable and acceptable to the employees, one which would have obviated the difficulties we have had. Had they done so, we would not require the kind of legislation we are debating today. For those reasons, we intend to vote against this bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few remarks on the bill introduced this afternoon by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) to provide for the resumption and continuation of postal services. Mr. Speaker, the House of Commons is faced this afternoon with quite a delicate problem, as we must choose between two priorities: on the one hand, the public's right to postal services, and on the other hand, the union's right to call a strike. On the one hand, we have 23 million persons entitled to postal services, and on the other, 23,000 workers to whom the government has granted the right to strike and is asking us today to take it away from them through Bill C-8.
Mr. Speaker, I have always believed that the rights of the majority should prevail over those of the minority, which does not prevent us to pass special legislation to protect minority rights.
In the public service we constantly see strikes which are brought to an end by special legislation. Often those special pieces of legislation entail large expenses. Fortunately we are in Ottawa today, but if we were in our constituencies we would have to leave and come to parliament to vote such a legislation to order Post Office strikers back to work. Moreover, I find it rather strange that the government has waited so long before telling us how serious this problem is.
I was listening a moment ago to the Acting Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet) who outlined to the House all the meetings he had with union leaders. In the course of those discussions, he told us that he had appointed conciliation boards, mediators, arbitrators and what have you. According to him, he did his utmost to try and arrange a reasonable solution, implying that the unions are the ones which are not reasonable. As for the spokesman for the official opposition party, all he said was: We have no other choice than vote for such a legislation since we are faced with a fait accompli, and he wished that legislation be brought in the House to avoid all those conflicts.
As usual, the New Democratic Party is in favour of upholding the right to strike and of giving unions everything they want in an attempt to calm them down. Well, it is the same old story and we find ourselves today in the same dilemma once again.
Mr. Speaker, if we pass this bill, is it going to solve the problem? If we were at least sure of it, it would not be a waste of time, but I am rather sure that the passage of this bill will not solve anything in the Post Office, as it has never solved anything in the public service in general. It is precisely that sector, of all public and extragovernmental sectors, Mr. Speaker, that has been the most troublesome in recent years and that has most affected our Canadian economy and hurt the Canadian people.
October 17, 1978

I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether parliamentarians will finally understand that it is impossible for a government which will be the judge to settle honestly a labour dispute while being both the employer and the accused. It is impossible, because too many interests are at stake. That is why we have always advocated and still do a non political organization beyond the control of the government which would settle those collective agreements. I have just found a newspaper report dated September 2, 1973, and there is nothing new, Mr. Speaker. Our demands are similar to those made by Real Caouette at that time, according to that article signed by Claude Lavergne and entitled: "The Prevention of Conflicts" in which reads, and I quote:
Anyhow, every time parliament is forced to step in and pass special legislation, the dispute is suddenly referred to an arbitration board whose award is binding and without appeal.
To be practical, one has to set the facts in their true light: either an agreement is reached through negotiation or arbitration and, then, the right to strike is of no use whatsoever, or a strike is called and then this right is withdrawn by a special legislation, which again makes it inoperative.
Why not take the easy way and set up regular and on going mechanisms in order to prevent a recurrence of the same problems?
The present policy is aimed at patching things up. The solution suggested by Real Caouette seeks a social and orderly peace through the prevention of conflicts.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I say again-and with this I know the unions will agree, for let no one think that I blame them alone-I say again that in any quarrel both sides are often wrong in some regards and right in others. It is up to the arbitrator to decide who of the two is right. I am all for protecting the right of the worker to his job. That is why I say that in the case of a civil servant, there can be no justice when the employer is the state which is both the accused and the judge at the same time. It cannot be both. That is why a court is an absolute necessity.
We demand the creation of a permanent court of arbitration whose decision would be binding and could not be appealed, a tribunal composed of three judges, one appointed by Parlie-ment and not a political party, another by the unions and the third to come from the public at large. That tribunal should be completely apolitical. In its actions, it could not be influenced by any political or union wave. It seems to me that would be the ideal tribunal for ensuring that justice is done in such cases by both the worker and the employer. And so the rights of the 23 million inhabitants of this country would be protected while those of the 23,000 postal employees would be respected.
Mr. Speaker, to my mind, that is the only way we can avoid coming back constantly to the House to pass back to work legislation for civil servants. That is the only way, there is no other. But which government will dare introduce such a bill? I wonder. We have been asking the Liberals for one for ten years now. Will another government finally give it to us, so that we can have both peace and justice in Canada at the same time? That is what I hope for as I ask the government if the
Postal Services
time has not come to act, to act now, and create such a tribunal?

Mr. Speaker, I will say just a few words during the presentation of this legislation. I just want to remind hon. members that when we are considering such a proposal, we should stop and think and ask why, for instance, in 1978, in a civilized country as advanced as ours, in a civilization which has some claims to progress and to development in every respect, how it happens that we have again to resolve through coercion such a simple problem as the services to be provided to a population. We should wonder why we have not yet found a means to prevent so many workers from relying on blackmail, which is what all those strikes are, as well as to prevent the government from resorting to more or less honest procedures which are very often childish, to say the least.
Mr. Speaker, we should certainly have found by now the means to prevent this situation from occurring. We should not try to find someone to blame. We should not try to find out precisely who is responsible for the situation, but rather, Mr. Speaker, we should find the means to settle this once and for all. This kind of blackmail should not exist in 1978. Such childishness should not occur in negotiations in 1978. Both parties should understand that there are strict rules that must be obeyed concerning ethics, respect and basic good manners. It is possible to assert your rights and even request certain privileges without annoying millions of people who need their mail. It is very well to request all that you desire, whether it be salary increases or better working conditions, but there is no need to do so by causing all sorts of disastrous problems for your neighbours.
Mr. Speaker, we must be sufficiently civilized to discover finally a basic formula which can eliminate all strikes in this country, to develop formulas, laws and regulations which can command respect. We now have a problem because our legislation and the principles behind it are inadequate and because no one wants to respect them. If only we really wanted to solve not only this problem and the present postal conflict, but all other similar problems because of which our population could not care less about problems! It is terrible, but this is what we have come to. How many times in the past have we seen people prepare themselves in anticipation of a future strike? For instance, the present strike does not bother at all those who have enough money to use special paid messenger services. Yes, we are so used to this situation that we have finally provided all sorts of alternatives in our own system. And while this goes on, we, the legislators duly mandated by the people, discuss another band-aid solution. Once again we discuss the means to solve a problem in the short term without thinking about the need to find a permanent solution.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that all this had to be said in this House during the debate on this bill. Of course, I agree that this problem must be solved. I agree completely as to the need to do so. However, what I want most is for us to insist from now on on finding the means to eliminate this situation so that we shall have fulfilled in this House our true responsibility towards the people we represent.

Mr. Chairman, as I indicated in my speech earlier today the main reason for this is to prevent an early recurrence of the present situation and to ensure, if possible, uninterrupted postal service during the transition period of the planned conversion of the post office to a Crown corporation.
The current collective agreement that we are discussing is one that will normally end at the end of the current year. We are dealing with this legislation today, in the middle of October. In order for the mediator-arbitrator to at least try to have genuine mediation take place, we feel we should give him a certain period of time to bring the parties together and try to mediate, if possible, particular clauses of the settlement.
This legislation states that if for certain reasons the mediation is not successful, this person will no longer act as a mediator but as an arbitrator in order to deal with the unresolved questions. In order for this mediator-arbitrator to do a fair job, we are giving him three months. That takes us into the early part of 1979.
We believe that extending the agreement to the end of 1979 will, as I said earlier, create a good climate for 1979 while parliament during the course of that year passes legislation to turn the post office into a Crown corporation. Another good reason for this extension is to allow the mediator-arbitrator some time to carry out his assignment and allow some time for the resulting collective agreement terms to take effect.
I appreciate that it is an unusual measure, an extraordinary measure in certain respects. However, I do not think it would be correct to ask parliament to pass such a provision at this time for an agreement that would be terminated in just a few weeks. This is why we recommend that the current collective agreement be extended to December 31, 1979.
I want it to be clearly understood that the mediator-arbitrator will not be subject to the anti-inflation clause for the year 1979. He will obviously be assisting the parties in a mediation role, trying to bring about a mutual agreement. If he cannot

Mr. Chairman, before the dinner hour we were discussing clause 5 which appears in the bill under the heading "Collective agreement" and carries the description "Term of collective agreement extended".
It is not unusual for the terms of a contract to be extended for a short period. This particular agreement ran out in July of 1977, I am told, and negotiations have been going on to the present time, the fall of 1978. Thus, a year and several months have gone by. In some cases when a contract has been extended we have specified that an agreement had to be reached within a certain period. The bill before us does say there has to be an agreement or at least a report on the terms of an agreement within 90 days. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the mediator-arbitrator concept is not brand new but has been in existence for many years, perhaps six, seven or eight. It has been used more often in the United States than in Canada. This approach has been used recently in Canada in relation to the longshoremen's settlement in the port of Montreal. It has also been used on three occasions in western Canada in respect of the grain handlers. It is called mediation-arbitration, and it is a proce-
October 17, 1978

dure whereby the parties arm a very skilled mediator with the power of an arbitrator, to be used if necessary.
The most important factor of this concept is that labour and management, while parties to an arbitration proceeding, still have the opportunity to carry on with the negotiation process. It seems to me there is great potential for this technique in situations where the parties realize that a strike will result in severe adverse effects on a country or on a community, and will in fact inflict more punishment on the public than on a party to the dispute. I must say that this dispute would come within that category.
This is obviously a relatively new concept and is not something that is used normally. However, it is a concept that allows parties having difficulty in arriving at negotiated settlements to receive the help of a third party who acts as mediator. He is a person who tries to obtain the co-operation of the parties to the dispute in arriving at a collective agreement. This third party is armed with clout in the sense that the third party is a person active in the course of the mediation taking place between the parties.
The parties must always remember in discussing aspects of the collective agreement that if they do not agree or do not furnish substantial evidence or do not argue successfully their case on why they advocate a clause or reject a demand the mediator will act later on in the process as an arbitrator, keeping in mind the positions advanced by both parties and rendering a decision which will be binding on both parties.
It is a new technique in Canada, but it is a technique that has been very helpful and useful in many respects in disputes in the United States. It is a technique which has become more and more useful in Canada, and we think that it will serve very well in the circumstances we are facing now.

This matter has now been raised for the second time. I believe the minister agrees that certain factors ought to be considered. If that is so, attention ought to be given to this clause. It is the government which will be appointing the members of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, so it is the government which will be negotiating, in effect, if this dispute is to be referred in the end to compulsory arbitration. Most hon. members are familiar with the dispute which took place in 1975 having to do with industrial change; it would be most unfair in my view if all the rewards gained by the workers following that dispute were to be taken away.
A few minutes ago, the hon. member for Vancouver South urged us to get on with this item of business because all we were doing was getting the post office workers back to work. Mr. Chairman, the Post Office has not worked for a long time. It takes seven or eight days to put a letter through the Toronto post office with all the machinery there. I see a number of officials in the gallery. They are on holiday, too, laughing and having a great time. They have been on holiday for five or six years in my opinion. We all know that mail service has deteriorated sharply.
It is reasonable, I think, for the public to know that the settlement we are imposing tonight is costing the workers a great deal. They made their proposal for a year's contract ending on July 1, 1978, and now we are extending it for another year and a half on the basis of the same proposals. It is all very well to say the workers should go back to work. We have to ask ourselves at what price, and if the minister is not willing to offer some of the concessions which are being requested and if we as members of parliament are unable to add to these clauses to allow other matters to be discussed in the interest of the employees, we are being very unfair.
I do not always agree with my hon. friend from Nickel Belt-
Aii hon. Member: Thank God!

Thank God on both sides. But in this instance I think he is right. Our objective should be not only to put people back to work in the post office and try to develop a spirit of harmony there; we must also make an effort to be fair and reasonable. We are not doing this.
No concession whatever is being made to the workers. After all, they have gone through the process of deciding whether they will take the strike route or the route of mediation or arbitration. They have made a legal choice. The union has done all the things it is asked to do and its members are now in a legal position to strike. Yet everything in this legislation is weighted on the other side. We are not taking into account the unfairness of the bargaining position. The minister is in a position, if he wishes, to provide a reasonable settlement as far as the workers are concerned, a contract covering three years. Maybe common sense does not prevail here either. It seems to me there are clauses in this bill which should be amended if it is really our wish to arrive at a settlement which would place
Postal Services
the post office in a position to carry on delivering the mail. Let us not make it inevitable that other action should take place in the post office which would be to the detriment of the public.
We could be exceedingly unfair to one side by way of legislation. By legislating high wages, as we have done once or twice in the past, the Post Office might have to double the price of a postage stamp. I remember that we legislated an increase of 30 cents in order to settle a strike on the seaway a number of years ago, and we started the whole inflation mess. If we are going to be unfair, we can expect those who are unfairly treated to react, and that would not be conducive to peace in the postal structure.
In fairness to the people concerned can we not give some consideration to allowing additional items to be added, as recommended in my colleague's motion? If that is not possible, can we not take away something which will be detrimental and costly to the employees of the post office? We are in a position to do that. As legislators we are in a position to be unfair as well, but it seems to me that it would be better for us to err on the side of fairness and justice than to err on the side of satisfying some civil servants who feel that some of the gains made by way of a previous strike should not have been allowed and who are now in a position to arbitrate them away.

Mr. Chairman, in the last 25 years we have seen a tremendous change in many industries in this country. I would remind the acting minister that in the mid-1960's, and the assistant deputy minister will remember this very well, we had a work stoppage on the CPR because the CPR unilaterally decided to extend the runs of engineers. This led to the appointment of Mr. Justice Freedman who held hearings on the matter and made some important and profound recommendations in respect of technological changes, some of which we have still not accepted.
The minister knows that in the city of Montreal the longshoremen's industry has changed dramatically as a result of the introduction of containerization. This has led to a very sharp decline in the number of longshoremen. The printing industry is also experiencing an industrial revolution because of the use of computers in the place of the old typographical machines.
There is no one change that concerns working people more than technological change. I thought we were dealing here with a bill which would give the mediator-arbitrator the authority to settle many of the questions that have not beer, agreed to by the post office and postal workers, such as the hourly rate of pay, the number of hours, rest periods and so on. Although I do not like this legislation and said we would vote against it, I was prepared to debate the matter today without a great deal of heat or rhetoric. I was shocked, therefore, to hear the minister indicate a moment ago that the mediator-arbitrator would have the authority to deal with clauses of the present agreement relating to technological change.
I do not want to make a long speech, but we are facing legislation on the first day of a strike. Somehow in 1978 we cannot have a strike in the post office that lasts more than one day. Back in 1975 we had a strike that lasted 43 days, and at that time the minister and the government said they were prepared to let it go on even longer.
One of the most important issues, if not the most important, in that earlier dispute related to the matter of technological change. As a result of that strike the workers obtained the right to negotiate when technological change took place. It may be that this is not working very well as far as the

employer is concerned, and I do not think it is working well as far as the employees are concerned. In any event, there is a right of negotiation in respect of technological change.
Now the minister tells us that the mediator-arbitrator will have the right to deal with this because the Public Service Staff Relations Board will have this matter as one that can be negotiated. Let us be realistic. We are passing legislation which gives the government the right to appoint the mediator-arbitrator. That is not a three-man board on which the employees have a representative, as they do on conciliation boards. This is a one-man board with the full power to settle these questions, and that one member is to be appointed by the government. Then another arm of the government, the Treasury Board, together with the Post Office Department, will appear before the arbitrator and argue that the clause in the agreement which was arrived at after a 43-day strike should be eliminated. If that happens, who could blame the workers if they felt that they had been dealt with by a kangaroo court?
If that is what this section provides and if that is the decision which the arbitrator will make, then in January of 1980 we will have another postal strike, and whoever is in parliament at that time will have to deal with it. 1 would urge the minister to use some common sense. Therefore, I propose an amendment which I think will take care of this difficulty and which is inherent in the legislation as it is written. I move: That clause 6(1) be amended on page 3 at line 13, by adding immediately after the word "thereof' the following words:
"provided, however, that no arbitral award shall impose terms or conditions of employment which take away rights enjoyed by the employee and employee organization pursuant to any of the provisions of the collective agreement."
I think that it would be an error of tremendous proportion for the government to use this occasion to take away from the worker unilaterally rights they obtained after a long strike at great cost to them and at great cost to the people as a whole and which they obtained through legitimate collective bargaining. It would not only be a disservice to the workers in the post office, but it would inevitably lead to a strike as soon as this legislation is passed.

Once you affect the security of employment, you attack and destroy the right of

We cannot have a situation where the mediator-arbitrator may withdraw things won and agreed upon in previous agreements, have him take something out and suggest to the House that that is going to create peace in the post office in the interim period before the Crown corporation comes into effect. Can you imagine the technological change clause being lifted and peace continuing within the post office?
It is important to note the words of one of the conciliation board members, Mr. Irving Gaul, the union nominee on the board. What he had to say in the conciliation report was very timely, and I would like to read it into the record:
Industrial peace is a prerequisite for the successful transition to Crown corporation status but industrial peace cannot be legislated by a parliamentary act. It can be achieved by the resolution of the problems, which can only be accomplished as a result of negotiated solutions.

It seems to me that that is the kernel to the problem. If the minister does not accept this amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, in effect he will not have industrial peace in the transitional period leading up to Crown corporation status. Surely, that has to be paramount in his mind. It would be a hoodwinking of the public if we let them think that what we do here tonight is somehow or other going to move the mail for the next year or two. Indeed, I think that what has been foisted on the taxpayers so far is a travesty.
I saw advertisements in the newspaper showing what the employer offered and what the employee wanted. About $300,000 was spent on a publicity campaign but did it bring peace to the post office? Was that money used to bring industrial peace to the post office? Should we use taxpayers' money to resolve those problems? It may have helped the government or the post office to wage a propaganda war for the public mind, but surely if the taxpayers' money is being spent it ought to be spent on the resolution of the problem and not to win public support for being such a good employer while implying that CUPW is a bunch of unreasonable people who want 30 hours of work for 40 hours' pay.
Surely the solutions do not lie in this open-ended kind of legislation which gives power to the arbitrator to remove things already won.
In the last contract CUPW thought the problem of casuals had been solved, but the post office kept circumventing the clauses in the agreement by not offering work to the full-time employees before hiring casuals. Grievances were built up and the matter was taken to the grievance board. We are here tonight in the hope that we can develop some sort of peace in the post office in the period before the establishment of a Crown corporation. We all know that the question of trust is important in collective bargaining. We could never use that word to describe collective bargaining with Treasury Board. Mr. Chairman, clause 6 is the key to the entire piece of legislation in many respects. It seems to me we are not getting many satisfactory replies from the minister or the government. The government has repeatedly said in this House that we are giving to the public service the right to bargain collectively regarding wages, hours and conditions of labour. We all recognize there are situations in which that right has been restricted and even withheld. That is what we are in the process of doing today.
Surely in the haste to withdraw that right in the public interest this House, this committee and the minister have a responsibility to ensure that we take adequate precautions to see that those whose rights are being denied are given some

compensation in the form of an assurance that the dispute will be adequately considered and fairly resolved.
I have seen this type of legislation passed a number of times but I have never seen it passed on the first day of a strike, never rushed through as quickly as this. The kernel of the matter is that the government will appoint a mediator-arbitrator who will have the sole power to decide issues respecting wages, hours of work and conditions of employment of the 23,000 postal employees for the next 15 months. The minister has not given us any guarantee that some of the rights they now enjoy will not be taken away.
We attempted to clarify that a few moments ago, but that amendment was smothered by the government and the official opposition. May we have some idea as to the type of person who will be chosen to discharge this very special responsibility? I am not asking for his name, but will he be a judge? That has been the case in the past. Will it be someone within the public service? Can he assure us that the person who is charged with this very heavy responsibility is a person in whom the 23,000 employees and the House can have confidence?
I am sure the minister agrees that the arbitrator's responsibility will be a heavy one. The minister will not be in a position to amend any of the arbitrator's decisions. In fact, none of us will have the power to amend any of his decisions. It is a tremendous responsibility for one man to have in the hollow of his hand, the well-being of those 23,000 employees for the next 15 months. Those employees have put their trust in the House. Can the minister tell us what type of person he will select? What safeguards will the employees have? Are they to be put back to work? We know they will be under the Anti-Inflation Act for the next 15 months. That is something most Canadian employees will not have to face.

speechtext: I suppose the only thing they will have to do is obey the law, Stanley.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I think we should have some respect around here for the laws we make. My hon. friend and the rest of us agreed today to interrupt the normal business of this House and to deal with this special bill, which is here for one purpose only, and that is to get the mails moving again. But here, tucked into this bill, is clause 10 which would amend the Public Service Staff Relations Act in respect of a very controversial provision in that act. I admit that I was the only member of the committee who voted against that report. The Liberals and the Conservatives all bought it, but surely it is a controversial provision like others, and I think that the idea of putting this in is completely wrong.
My hon. friend says that the postal employees can avoid these penalties by obeying the law. That is a plausible, under-
Postal Services
standable statement, but I suggest to him-and he is a lawyer-that what they ought to be required to meet by way of penalties are the penalties that are in the law now, the penalties which were in the law when they went on strike. That was the law yesterday. It will be the law until this law is passed. There are certain penalties, but if this bill is passed by this House tonight, passed by the other place and becomes law in 24 or 48 hours, postal workers will discover that between the time they legally went on strike and the time they are told that they have to go back to work the penalties will have been increased. I think that is completely wrong. I think it is contrary to the whole concept of law, and that in itself makes it wrong.
In addition to that, I say that it is quite offensive to this House and to the whole parliamentary practice to import into a special, emergency piece of legislation a major amendment of general and lasting application to the fundamental laws of this country. The minister has done fairly well in the last hour in terms of accepting some suggestions from this side of the House. I regret that he turned down the most important one, but he has accepted a number of amendments, and I seriously appeal to him to agree to withdrawing clause 10 from this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is important that the bill with which we are now dealing not be frustrated in its application by the enforcement deficiencies of the Public Service Staff Relations Act which were recognized by the joint committee. This House owes it to the public to seize the very first opportunity we have to correct the situation and bring about some of the recommendations which were made by the joint committee on employer-employee relations in the public service.
I appreciate that at the time this question was studied by the joint committee the hon. member voted against this recommendation, but I think there was an overwhelming majority of members on that committee who worked very hard and conscientiously and thought that something ought to be done to make sure that these remedies which we are considering are there to allow for a minimum of disrespect for the law. I think this clause is part and parcel of this bill, and the intention is to get the mails moving again in the near future.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with care to the point made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. It seems to me that the point is very crucial. This is not the first time that a person who is not a lawyer has corrected lawyers in this House on a question of justice. Canadians as well as people in other countries learned a long time ago never to confuse legal statements with statements about justice.
Surely the fundamental point which was being made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was that we have a perfect example here of ex post facto law. A group of men and women have exercised their rights under laws which exist in Canada and have embarked on a strike. They are legally involved in this strike, and now if we in this parliament pass this particular provision, we are coming along and saying that in the process we are going to change the punishment if the

October 17, 1978
Postal Services
law is violated. A fundamental concept of justice and law in this land is that you do not do that kind of thing. You do not say to a group of men and women when they embark on a certain course of action: "This is the law as it exists, but we are going to change the law in terms of this provision once you have started to exercise your legal right".
There is no question about the right of parliament in this or any other matter to pass the kind of law which is being advocated by the minister, but it seems to me that those who are concerned about basic principles of justice ought not to be supporting this principle at this time. If the minister wanted to raise the level of punishment for violation of law in this respect or any other, surely the time to do that is before workers involved in a strike have exercised their legal right so to act. I wish the minister would deal with precisely that point in his response. Are we not changing the rules of the game in midstream and, if so, how does he justify that?
I will not elaborate on my second point. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made the point very clearly. We are making a permanent change in legislation here, quite apart from the postal workers, on the whole question-

subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext: No, we are not. Read it. It only affects postal workers.

subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext: -of punishment for workers in the public service, and it seems to me that this is not the appropriate time to do that. The time to do that would be when we have proper amendments brought before the House which pertain to existing legal provisions. We should not deal with this matter in the context of a strike which is now in progress.

subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it may have been inadvertent on the part of the Leader of the New Democratic Party when he said, as I think one other hon. member said earlier, that clause 10 would amend the Public Service Staff Relations Act for all other public servants. I certainly do not read it that way. If we read it carefully, I think we will find that it applies only to the particular collective agreement with which this bill deals. I want to ask if the minister would confirm that my impression is the same impression he has. Perhaps he can answer that in a moment.
I want to say something else. The fact is that a number of members of parliament of all parties took a look at the penalty provisions of the Public Service Staff Relations Act, and since several years ago they have been deemed inadequate. There was an almost unanimous decision that they should be changed.
I have listened with sympathy to my hon. friends who have just argued, but there is an obligation on this House to ensure that the law which is passed tonight will be taken seriously. I have to say to the acting minister and to the Postmaster General that our party supports this amendment and that many members of this House have given a great deal of consideration to it in the past.
I do not want the acting minister to think that I allow small errors to go unnoticed, so I say to him that I agree with my

colleague, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, that we are bootlegging in one provision and not dealing in a cohesive manner with other provisions. However, as the minister has acknowledged tonight, there seems to be some awareness of that on the government side of the House as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the intervention of the hon. member for Vancouver South. He just said what I was going to say as a matter of clarification. This clause refers specifically to whom this act applies, namely those who are touched by this collective agreement.
In order to have more clarification about this clause, one has to go back to the definitions, such as you find in clause 2 where it is quite clear that we are referring to employees, who are defined in the clause, and employees' organizations, which are also defined there. Therefore, no one should think that we are amending section 104 of the Public Service Staff Relations Act to deal with all the other collective agreements which are in existence at present. It is indeed a measure which is restricted at this moment, but it could be dealt with more generally later on when the government will be dealing with something more specific than the amendment to the Public Service Staff Relations Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hate to belabour this point. The point in question is that we are now attempting to govern by intimidation. Nobody questions-at least I do not, nor do 1 think the leader of the NDP questions for one moment-the wording in the act and its narrow restriction to the matter before us. But I must agree with him, and 1 think he is right in saying, that you are governing by intimidation.
We have a strike of engineers presently, a legal situation. They will wake up tomorrow morning and take a look at the fines in this legislation. That is intimidation. I do not like it, I reject it, and please do not pass it off simply as being a necesary action so as to enforce the serious decision of this chamber. The law itself must carry its own weight. If, because we have no faith in the leadership of CUPW or of the unions involved to obey the law, we have to impose a fine, then let it stand by itself. Let us not duck the factual situation-

subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, tell him to sit down or get out. One of those assholes up there is waving, shouting and making signals.

subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Let them do their waving and signalling; it is the Post Office we are talking about. The Post Office has been waving and signalling to Canadians for years. That is what we are doing here tonight.
The point I want to make through you, Mr. Chairman-I think it is fairly serious-is that I have no hesitation whatsoever in passing this, absolutely none. Indeed, I agree with it. What I am saying to you is that tomorrow morning when we wake up, we can impose no lesser penalty for any offence, for any infringement of any act involving parliament, government, and its employees.

Surely we are not talking about the Star Chamber. In this penalty clause we say to every employee of the public service of Canada: This is the precedent. I accepted it, I voted for it, and the minister's colleague sitting immediately behind him will indicate to him exactly where that clause was written, on whose coffee table, after what consultation and with what unions. But let us make no mistake about it, and I am sure the distinguished Leader of the NDP is not under any illusions about it; nor, I am sure, is the Prime Minister of this country.

speechtext: Don't be too sure about that.

subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext: The member for Dartmouth-Halifax East is not, and I would remind all hon. members that I do not think there is any mistake about it at all. We are legislating ad hoc. It does not matter what the term is. We are saying very clearly to the public servants of this country, to the people who work for the people of this country, that these are the penalties, and let us be aware of that. We are also implying that there can be no lesser penalties from this point on.

Mr. Chairman, I am puzzled by this clause. I have asked my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who has been here a long time, whether he remembers a single case in his long experience when parliament passed a law ordering a union, a group of workers, to go back to work and that law was defied by the union. My colleague tells me he does not remember a single such case.
That being the situation, I find it strange that the minister brings in a clause in this bill which is as tough as it is. I think I have a right to say this to the minister: I compare this legislation containing pretty tough penalties for workers who have never defied the law with the way we have treated corporations in this country for 50 years, corporations which have, not once and not twice, but innumerable times, deliberately, and in conspiracy with each other, violated the combines act.

subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext: The sugar companies.

subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICES
speechtext: It was not until this year that the courts directed the companies to pay a fine which meant anything to them. So for 50 years we have allowed the corporations of this country to violate our laws, to steal from the people of Canada, to set prices in ways which were illegal, and we have done virtually nothing about it until this year. Not a single corporation officer has never gone to prison for breaking the law. We have corporations-I am sure the minister knows it-which have broken those laws, not once but twice or three times. But when it comes to groups of workers who, to my knowledge, have never defied a law ordering them back to work, the minister decides in advance that that union may indeed defy the law and therefore imposes penalties which have never been necessary until now. I find that very strange. I also find it very strange that the minister sits in his chair so frequently tonight and does not reply.

I think I have already explained the reason why this clause is in the bill. To have the hon. member suggest
Postal Services
that I sit in my chair and do not answer him and for him to imply that I do not want to answer is incorrect. Indeed, I have made replies on three previous occasions to this question. Obviously every hon. member is entitled to speak on this clause and to bring forward arguments for or against such a clause. But I do not think I ought to reply to every member who presents an argument for or against.
I suspect that members of this committee are by now fully aware of the reasons this clause is included. I know some members are opposed to it and I respect their view. I know, on the other hand, there are a number of members who favour the inclusion of this clause, which increases the penalties for those who will not obey the law. I hope and assume that all members of this committee expect that this law will be obeyed.
Basically I do not agree with the interventions made earlier by the hon. member to the effect that we are intimidating the employees. I do not think this is an intimidation at all, but rather a clause that increases the penalties. These penalties are increased following the considerations of a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate, a committee which came forward some time ago with a recommendation to increase the penalties. The penalties will now be increased and we hope this law will be obeyed. If it is not obeyed, the penalties are greater than they were before, and I believe there are arguments for and against doing this. I respect the view expressed by the hon. member, but surely he should not think that every time someone disagrees I should stand up and make another speech.

Mr. Chairman, we cannot look at this particular clause regarding punishment for disobedience of the law in isolation. This is another piece of nastiness in this bill which we have to look at in relation to other aspects. This gives one the impression that the government is spoiling for a fight, and that in fact it is another attempt at confrontation politics.
We discovered earlier tonight that a mediator-arbitrator will be appointed. It has also been evident that this person will have a lot of power. We discovered that the minister and the government are not prepared to accept amendments which would in fact state that whatever the workers have achieved in the past will be protected. These things are all now up for grabs. The mediator-arbitrator may very well redefine technological change. The hon. member for Longueuil is shaking his head back and forth like a jack-in-the-box. The minister has already said this is a possibility and that the mediator-arbitrator would have that power. He may very well have the power to change the definition of technological change and the right to negotiate in respect of such change, which was agreed to after a 43-day strike.
We learned earlier his evening that the minister and the government refuse to accept an amendment to the bill which would spell out that the mediator-arbitrator will look at everything in this agreement and not just those matters referred by the Public Service Staff Relations Board to the conciliation board. Here again is another piece of nastiness which leads me

October 17, 1978
Postal Services
to the conclusion that this government is looking for a fight. It seems to me this is one way of instigating disobedience. I have only been here six years but I do not recall public servants defying the law or disobeying parliament. Yet we have this clause thrown into this bill in respect of this group of workers. The government is singling out the members of CUPW to show the Canadian public how tough it is. After one day of strike the government is showing the people of Canada how tough it can be.
Perhaps the government is a day late in its attempt to prevent the by-election fiasco of yesterday. It seems to me this is the wrong way to go about obtaining industrial peace during this period of time before moving to a Crown corporation. This certainly gives the impression to the workers who are to be put back to work they are being put upon by this legislation in that several of those things they won in the past as a result of hard negotiations may be removed.
It seems to me what we are doing here tonight is sowing the seeds of discontent for years to come. It is quite possible this parliament may, if it passes this legislation, sour the possibility of Crown corporation success in the future because trust is not being established. All we are doing is institutionalizing the distrust and anger of the workers in the Post Office.

I suggest there is nothing more aggravating to the situation than disobedience of a law. The hon. member in moving such an amendment and in opposing the bill takes for granted that the workers will be disobedient. I should like to think that they will not.
I should like to think also that in coming months we will be dealing with important labour relations in the Post Office, specifically with a bill to create a Crown corporation. These penalties are there to make sure that this bill will not be frustrated in its application, and there are proper measures to make sure that it is applicable. Therefore, I cannot agree with this amendment.
